items.gloss_md: Sequencing of (reverse-transcribed) RNA to measure which transcripts are present in a sample and how abundant they are.
items.body_md:
RNA is extracted, mRNA enriched (poly-A selection) or rRNA removed, fragmented, reverse-transcribed to cDNA, ligated to adapters and sequenced, usually on Illumina short-read instruments (e.g. 2×100–150 bp, ~20–50 million reads per sample for differential expression). Reads are aligned to a genome (STAR, HISAT2) or pseudo-aligned to a transcriptome (salmon, kallisto) and counted per gene or transcript.

- Measures: expression of all genes at once, plus splicing, isoforms, fusions, allele-specific expression, expressed variants and novel transcripts.
- Advantages over microarrays: no predefined probes, larger dynamic range, works for any organism.
- Variants: stranded/unstranded, poly-A vs total RNA, 3' tag, small RNA, long-read, targeted panels, single-cell and spatial versions.
- Limitations: counts are relative (compositional), depend on library size and gene length (hence TPM/CPM and DESeq2/edgeR normalisation), batch effects, RNA quality (RIN/DV200).

Introduced in 2008 (e.g. Mortazavi et al., Nagalakshmi et al.); today the default for bulk transcriptomics. Standard analysis: count matrix → DESeq2/edgeR/limma-voom differential expression → gene-set enrichment.

attrs.mnemonic: RNA-seq counts reads, not molecules: the more reads a gene 'eats' (long gene, deep library), the more it seems expressed – that is why you always normalise.
attrs.anecdote: Mortazavi et al. (2008, Wold lab), 'Mapping and quantifying mammalian transcriptomes by RNA-Seq', popularised the name and introduced RPKM – a unit later criticised as inconsistent between samples and largely replaced by TPM.

items.gloss_md: A glass slide or chip with thousands of immobilised DNA probes to which labelled sample cDNA/cRNA hybridises, so that fluorescence intensity reports the abundance of each transcript.
items.body_md:
Principle: RNA is converted to labelled cDNA or cRNA, hybridised to complementary probes (25–60-mer oligonucleotides) at defined positions, washed and scanned; the fluorescence per probe is proportional (non-linearly) to transcript abundance.

- Platforms: Affymetrix/Thermo Fisher GeneChip (one-colour, short in-situ-synthesised probes, e.g. HG-U133 Plus 2.0, Clariom), Illumina BeadArray/BeadChip (beads with 50-mer probes), Agilent (60-mer probes, two-colour or one-colour).
- Data: log2 intensities; preprocessing with background correction, normalisation (RMA, quantile) and probe summarisation; differential expression typically with limma.
- Strengths: cheap, robust, standardised, huge public archives (GEO, ArrayExpress), many legacy clinical cohorts.
- Limitations: only predefined probes, cross-hybridisation, background and saturation limit the dynamic range, poor for low-abundance and novel transcripts, platform-specific probe annotation.

Developed in the mid-1990s (cDNA spotted arrays from Pat Brown's lab at Stanford, Schena et al. 1995; Affymetrix photolithographic arrays). Largely replaced by RNA-seq for discovery, but still used and important for re-analysing archived datasets.

attrs.mnemonic: Microarray = 'pre-ordered menu': you only measure what has a probe on the chip. RNA-seq = 'à la carte': you see whatever is in the sample.
attrs.anecdote: Pat Brown's lab published free instructions for building a home-made arrayer ('the MGuide'), so academic labs could spot their own cDNA arrays instead of buying expensive commercial chips.

items.gloss_md: PCR in which the amplification is monitored by fluorescence in every cycle, so the starting amount of a DNA (or, after reverse transcription, RNA) target can be quantified.
items.body_md:
Fluorescence (SYBR Green dye or a sequence-specific probe such as TaqMan) increases with product; the cycle at which it crosses a threshold is the Ct (or Cq) value. Fewer cycles = more template: one cycle difference ≈ twofold difference at 100 % efficiency.

- RT-qPCR: RNA is first reverse-transcribed to cDNA (one-step or two-step) to measure gene expression; it is the gold standard for validating RNA-seq/microarray results of a few genes.
- Quantification: relative (ΔΔCt against reference genes and a control sample) or absolute (standard curve). Digital PCR gives absolute counts without a curve.
- Strengths: very sensitive (single copies), fast, cheap per target, wide dynamic range (~7–8 logs), clinical standard (viral load, e.g. HBV/HCV/CMV in transplant patients; SARS-CoV-2).
- Limitations: few targets per reaction, depends on primer efficiency and reference-gene stability; good practice is described in the MIQE guidelines (2009).

Note the naming trap: "RT-PCR" means reverse-transcription PCR; real-time PCR is better called qPCR.

attrs.mnemonic: Ct = 'cycles till threshold': low Ct = lots of template (it crossed the line early), high Ct = little template.
attrs.anecdote: Kary Mullis conceived PCR in 1983 while driving at night along a California highway and received the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; real-time monitoring was added by Russell Higuchi and colleagues in the early 1990s with a video camera filming ethidium-bromide fluorescence.

items.gloss_md: Relative qPCR quantification: normalise the target Ct to a reference gene (ΔCt), compare to a control sample (ΔΔCt), and report fold change as 2^−ΔΔCt.
items.body_md:
Steps: ΔCt = Ct(target) − Ct(reference gene); ΔΔCt = ΔCt(sample) − ΔCt(control/calibrator); fold change = 2^−ΔΔCt.

- Assumes near-100 % and equal amplification efficiency of target and reference (each cycle doubles the product); if efficiencies differ, use the Pfaffl method or a standard curve.
- Statistics are best done on ΔCt values (log scale), then back-transformed.
- Reference genes must be stable across conditions (validate with geNorm/NormFinder; ideally use several).

Described by Livak and Schmittgen (2001), one of the most cited methods papers in biology.

attrs.mnemonic: Minus because lower Ct means more: 2^−ΔΔCt turns 'fewer cycles' into 'more expression'.
attrs.anecdote: Livak & Schmittgen's 2001 Methods paper describing 2^−ΔΔCt has been cited well over 100,000 times.

items.label_md: TaqMan probe vs SYBR Green detection
items.gloss_md: The two main qPCR detection chemistries: a sequence-specific hydrolysis probe (TaqMan) or a dye that binds any double-stranded DNA (SYBR Green).
items.body_md:
- TaqMan (5' nuclease / hydrolysis probe): an oligo with a 5' reporter fluorophore and a 3' quencher binds between the primers; the 5'→3' exonuclease activity of Taq polymerase cleaves it during extension, separating reporter from quencher. Very specific, allows multiplexing with different dyes, also used for SNP genotyping; costs more per assay.
- SYBR Green: intercalates into any dsDNA, cheap and flexible, but also detects primer dimers and off-target products, so a melt-curve analysis is required.
- Other probe chemistries: molecular beacons, Scorpions, hybridisation (FRET) probes.

TaqMan assays (Thermo Fisher/Applied Biosystems) are the de-facto standard for gene-expression and clinical assays.

attrs.mnemonic: TaqMan is named after Pac-Man: Taq polymerase 'eats' the probe and the light comes out.
attrs.anecdote: The name TaqMan really was a nod to the Pac-Man video game, because Taq polymerase chews through the probe.

items.gloss_md: PCR in which the sample is split into thousands to millions of partitions, each amplified to an end-point positive/negative result, so target copies are counted absolutely using Poisson statistics.
items.body_md:
Partitions are droplets (droplet digital PCR, Bio-Rad QX200/QX600) or nanowells/chips (Qiagen QIAcuity, Thermo Fisher QuantStudio Absolute Q). The fraction of positive partitions gives copies per µL via a Poisson correction.

- Strengths: absolute quantification without a standard curve, high precision, robust to PCR inhibitors, detects rare variants down to ~0.1 % or lower variant allele fraction.
- Uses: circulating tumour DNA (e.g. KRAS G12D/V/R in PDAC liquid biopsy), donor-derived cell-free DNA after transplantation, copy-number variation, viral load, NGS library quantification.
- Limitations: few targets per reaction, limited dynamic range at very high concentrations, more expensive than qPCR.

Concept proposed in the 1990s (Vogelstein and Kinzler coined "digital PCR", 1999); droplet systems became widespread from about 2011.

attrs.mnemonic: Digital = 0 or 1 per droplet: count the ones, not the curve.
attrs.anecdote: Vogelstein and Kinzler introduced 'digital PCR' in 1999 to find rare KRAS mutations in stool DNA of colorectal cancer patients.

items.gloss_md: A gene assumed to be stably expressed across samples and conditions, used to normalise qPCR (and sometimes NanoString) expression measurements.
items.body_md:
Classic choices: GAPDH, ACTB (β-actin), B2M, HPRT1, TBP, RPLP0, PPIA, 18S rRNA. None is universally stable: GAPDH changes with metabolism and hypoxia, ACTB with cytoskeletal remodelling, so stability has to be checked for each tissue and condition (e.g. liver fibrosis, tumour vs normal).

- Tools: geNorm, NormFinder, BestKeeper; MIQE recommends several validated reference genes and reporting how they were chosen.
- In Western blots the analogous "loading controls" (β-actin, GAPDH, tubulin, or better total-protein stain) serve the same purpose.

items.gloss_md: The dominant one-colour expression microarray platform, with short (25-mer) oligonucleotide probes synthesised in situ on the chip by photolithography; now sold by Thermo Fisher.
items.body_md:
Probes are built base by base using light-directed synthesis through masks. Each transcript is measured by a probe set of ~11 probe pairs (classic 3' arrays: perfect-match PM and mismatch MM probes) or many probes along the gene (whole-transcript arrays).

- Classic 3' IVT arrays: HG-U133A, HG-U133 Plus 2.0 (GPL570), hybridised with biotin-labelled cRNA, stained with streptavidin-phycoerythrin, scanned; raw files are .CEL.
- Whole-transcript (WT) arrays: Human Exon 1.0 ST, Human Gene 1.0/2.0 ST, Clariom S and Clariom D.
- Processing: RMA (most common), MAS5, GCRMA; probe-set annotation via Bioconductor annotation packages or custom CDFs (BrainArray).

Affymetrix was acquired by Thermo Fisher Scientific in 2016. Huge legacy datasets (TCGA precursors, many liver and PDAC cohorts in GEO) use these arrays.

attrs.mnemonic: Affy = 'photo-printed' chip: the probes are made like computer chips, with light and masks.
attrs.anecdote: Stephen Fodor and colleagues borrowed photolithography from the semiconductor industry (Science 1991), which is why the product was called a 'GeneChip'.

items.gloss_md: Affymetrix's most widely used human 3' expression array, with 54,675 probe sets covering about 47,000 transcripts (GEO platform GPL570).
items.body_md:
- Released in 2003; 25-mer PM/MM probe pairs (11 per probe set), targeting the 3' ends of transcripts with IVT-labelled cRNA.
- Probe-set IDs such as 201746_at; suffixes indicate specificity: _at (unique), _s_at (matches several transcripts, often of related genes), _x_at (may cross-hybridise).
- Many genes have several probe sets with different behaviour; collapsing to genes (max mean, or custom BrainArray CDF) is an analysis choice.
- GPL570 is the single largest platform in GEO, so it underlies many public meta-analyses and signatures (including well-known PDAC subtype data sets and liver cohorts).

attrs.mnemonic: GPL570 – the '570' you will meet in every GEO search for human arrays.

items.label_md: Affymetrix Clariom and Human Gene ST arrays
items.gloss_md: Thermo Fisher's whole-transcript microarrays (Human Gene 1.0/2.0 ST, Clariom S, Clariom D) with probes along the whole transcript instead of only the 3' end.
items.body_md:
- Whole-transcript labelling with random priming gives probe signal along the full transcript, less sensitive to 3' bias and partially degraded RNA.
- Human Exon 1.0 ST and Human Gene 1.0/2.0 ST: exon- and gene-level designs (2007–2011).
- Clariom S: gene-level, ~20,000 well-annotated genes, compact and cheap, also as 96-well plate arrays.
- Clariom D: transcript/exon-level with >500,000 transcripts, for alternative splicing analysis.
- Analysed with RMA via the oligo package (Bioconductor) or Transcriptome Analysis Console (TAC).

items.gloss_md: Illumina's microarray technology in which randomly placed 3-µm beads carrying gene-specific 50-mer probes sit in microwells and are decoded by an address sequence.
items.body_md:
Each bead type carries a 50-mer target probe plus an address sequence; beads self-assemble randomly in wells and are decoded after manufacture; each probe is present on ~15–30 beads, giving internal technical replicates.

- Expression BeadChips: HumanHT-12 (12 samples per chip, ~47,000 probes), HumanWG-6, MouseWG-6; data as probe-level or summarised intensities, preprocessed with neqc/limma or lumi.
- The same bead platform underlies Infinium SNP genotyping arrays (GWAS) and the Infinium methylation arrays (450K, EPIC).
- Expression BeadChips are no longer a main product, but many cohorts (e.g. blood transcriptomics) in GEO used them.

items.gloss_md: Microarray with 60-mer inkjet-synthesised probes on which two samples labelled with Cy3 (green) and Cy5 (red) are hybridised competitively to the same array.
items.body_md:
- Output is the log-ratio M = log2(Cy5/Cy3) per probe (and the average intensity A); MA-plots and loess normalisation correct intensity-dependent dye bias.
- Designs: reference design (every sample vs a common reference RNA) or loop/direct designs; dye swaps balance dye-specific effects.
- Agilent arrays (SurePrint) are also used in one-colour mode, and for array CGH (copy number) and miRNA profiling.
- Analysis classically with limma (Bioconductor), which grew out of two-colour array analysis.

Two-colour spotted cDNA arrays were the original Stanford microarray format; Agilent industrialised the approach with in-situ-synthesised long oligos.

attrs.mnemonic: Red over green: Cy5 is red, Cy3 is green – 'five is fire'.

items.gloss_md: The standard preprocessing of Affymetrix arrays: background correction, quantile normalisation and median-polish summarisation of probes into log2 probe-set expression values.
items.body_md:
Three steps:
1. Background correction of PM intensities with a normal + exponential convolution model (MM probes ignored).
2. Quantile normalisation, which forces all arrays to have identical intensity distributions.
3. Summarisation per probe set on the log2 scale with Tukey's median polish (robust to outlier probes).

- Published by Irizarry et al. (2003); implemented in the Bioconductor packages affy and oligo.
- Alternatives: MAS5 (Affymetrix's own, per-array), GCRMA (uses probe sequence), fRMA and SCAN for single-array processing.
- Caveat: quantile normalisation assumes most genes do not change and that global distributions are comparable – violated, e.g., with global transcriptional shifts.

attrs.mnemonic: RMA = Remove background, Make quantiles equal, Average robustly (median polish).

items.gloss_md: Enrichment of polyadenylated RNA (mainly mRNA) with oligo(dT) beads before RNA-seq, removing ribosomal RNA, which makes up ~80–90 % of total RNA.
items.body_md:
- Captures mature mRNAs and polyadenylated lncRNAs; misses non-polyadenylated RNAs (replication-dependent histone mRNAs, many ncRNAs, most pre-mRNA introns, circRNAs).
- Requires intact RNA (RIN ≥ ~7): with degraded RNA only fragments close to the poly(A) tail are captured, producing strong 3' bias.
- Gives high exonic read fraction and clean gene quantification at modest depth; the standard for good-quality fresh/frozen samples and cell lines (e.g. Illumina TruSeq Stranded mRNA, NEBNext Poly(A) mRNA).
- Also the basis of most single-cell methods (oligo-dT capture).

attrs.mnemonic: Poly-A grabs the tail – so it needs an intact animal: no tail, no catch (degraded RNA gives 3' bias).

items.gloss_md: Removal of rRNA from total RNA by probe hybridisation and capture or RNase H digestion, so that all other RNA species, including non-polyadenylated and pre-mRNA, can be sequenced.
items.body_md:
- Kits: Illumina Ribo-Zero Plus, NEBNext rRNA Depletion, KAPA RiboErase, QIAseq FastSelect; whole-blood protocols additionally remove globin mRNA.
- Keeps lncRNAs, histone mRNAs, circRNAs, nascent and intronic reads (useful for splicing kinetics and intron-based expression).
- Works with degraded and FFPE RNA because it does not depend on an intact poly(A) tail – the default for many clinical archival samples.
- Downsides: more reads needed (a large intronic fraction), residual rRNA if depletion fails, mitochondrial rRNA must also be targeted.

Often called "total RNA-seq"; compare poly(A) selection.

attrs.mnemonic: Poly-A picks what you want; rRNA depletion throws away what you don't want – and keeps everything else.

items.gloss_md: RNA-seq library preparation that preserves which DNA strand a transcript came from, so reads can be assigned to sense or antisense transcripts.
items.body_md:
- Most common method: dUTP second-strand marking – dUTP is incorporated into the second cDNA strand, which is then not amplified; with the usual Illumina protocols (TruSeq Stranded) read 1 maps to the antisense strand ("reverse" stranded; featureCounts -s 2, salmon ISR).
- Benefits: correctly quantifies overlapping genes on opposite strands and antisense transcripts/lncRNAs; better annotation of novel transcripts.
- Unstranded libraries (older protocols) lose this information; most current kits are stranded, so check strandedness when re-analysing data (e.g. with RSeQC infer_experiment or salmon's automatic detection).

items.gloss_md: Quality metrics for RNA: RIN scores degradation from 1 (degraded) to 10 (intact) from the electropherogram; DV200 is the percentage of RNA fragments longer than 200 nucleotides.
items.body_md:
- RIN is computed by the Agilent Bioanalyzer (RIN^e/RQN on TapeStation/Fragment Analyzer) from the whole electrophoretic trace, especially the 28S and 18S rRNA peaks.
- Typical cut-offs: RIN ≥ 7 for poly(A) RNA-seq; lower RIN causes 3' bias and fewer usable reads.
- DV200 is the preferred metric for FFPE RNA, where RIN is uninformative (usually 2–3); e.g. DV200 > 30–50 % is often required for capture-based RNA-seq.
- RNA quality is a frequent hidden confounder: if RIN differs between groups, it can masquerade as biology – include it as a covariate or check it.

Liver and especially pancreas tissue degrade quickly (pancreatic acinar cells are full of RNases), so fast snap-freezing matters.

attrs.mnemonic: RIN 10 = 'perfect ten', RIN 1 = 'RNA soup'.
attrs.anecdote: The pancreas is notorious among RNA biologists: it produces so much RNase that pancreatic RNase A from cattle was the enzyme with which Anfinsen did his Nobel-winning protein folding experiments.

items.gloss_md: Strategies to sequence the fragmented, chemically modified RNA from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue, typically using hybrid capture of coding exons or rRNA depletion instead of poly(A) selection.
items.body_md:
- Problem: formalin crosslinks and fragments RNA (RIN ~2), oligo(dT) capture fails; deamination artefacts appear.
- Exome-capture RNA-seq: random-primed cDNA is enriched with biotinylated probes against coding exons (Illumina TruSeq RNA Exome, formerly RNA Access; Illumina RNA Prep with Enrichment; Agilent SureSelect XT HS2 RNA). Robust with DV200 ≥ ~30 % and low input.
- Alternatives: rRNA depletion total RNA-seq, 3' tag methods, probe-based targeted panels (NanoString nCounter, 10x Flex, GeoMx), all of which tolerate fragmentation.
- Benefit: unlocks the huge pathology archives with long clinical follow-up (e.g. resected PDAC cohorts, explant livers).

items.gloss_md: Low-cost bulk RNA-seq that sequences only one read per transcript near its 3' end (oligo-dT priming), which suffices for gene-level expression counting.
items.body_md:
- Lexogen QuantSeq FWD/REV is the best-known kit; others: SMART-3SEQ, BRB-seq, Lexogen QuantSeq-Pool.
- Each transcript gives roughly one read regardless of length, so no length normalisation is needed; ~2–10 million reads per sample are enough.
- Strengths: cheap, high throughput, tolerant of partially degraded RNA, easy to multiplex – ideal for large screens, time courses and drug-response studies.
- Limitations: no isoform, splicing, fusion or variant information; depends on good 3' UTR annotation; strand-specific.

Single-cell droplet methods (10x 3') use the same principle.

items.gloss_md: A 3' bulk RNA-seq method that adds a sample barcode and UMI during reverse transcription so that many samples are pooled right away and prepared as one library.
items.body_md:
- Adapted from single-cell protocols: barcoded oligo-dT primers in the RT step, early pooling of up to ~100s of samples, then one tagmentation-based library.
- Cost per sample a fraction of standard RNA-seq; performs comparably for gene-level differential expression.
- Developed in the Deplancke lab (Alpern et al., Genome Biology 2019); commercialised by Alithea Genomics (MERCURIUS BRB-seq).
- Related approaches: Prime-seq, DRUG-seq (for compound screens), PLATE-seq.

items.gloss_md: RNA-seq of short RNAs (~18–40 nt) – mainly microRNAs, but also piRNAs, snoRNA and tRNA fragments – using size selection and direct adapter ligation.
items.body_md:
- Workflow: total RNA → 3' and 5' adapter ligation (exploiting the 5' phosphate and 3' OH of miRNAs) → RT-PCR → size selection (gel or beads) → short single-end reads (~50 bp).
- Analysis: adapter trimming, mapping to miRBase/genome, counting mature miRNAs and isomiRs (miRNA variants with shifted ends).
- Biases: ligation efficiency differs strongly between sequences (randomised adapter ends reduce this); 2'-O-methylated RNAs (plant miRNAs, piRNAs) ligate poorly.
- Alternatives for miRNAs: stem-loop RT-qPCR, NanoString nCounter miRNA panels, microarrays.
- Clinical interest: circulating miRNAs as biomarkers, e.g. the hepatocyte-specific miR-122 rises in serum with liver injury.

attrs.mnemonic: miR-122 = the liver's 'own' miRNA: think '1-2-2, the liver talks to you'.

items.gloss_md: Sequencing of the ~30-nt mRNA fragments protected by translating ribosomes from nuclease digestion, giving a genome-wide snapshot of translation.
items.body_md:
- Workflow: arrest translation (e.g. cycloheximide), digest unprotected RNA with RNase I, isolate monosomes, purify ribosome-protected fragments (RPFs, ~28–30 nt), convert to a sequencing library.
- Read positions show 3-nt periodicity (codon by codon); harringtonine or lactimidomycin treatment marks initiation sites.
- Applications: translation efficiency (RPF / mRNA-seq), discovery of novel ORFs (upstream ORFs, small ORFs, micropeptides), ribosome pausing, effects of drugs or stress (e.g. mTOR inhibition).
- Introduced by Ingolia, Weissman et al. (Science 2009).

attrs.anecdote: Ribosome footprinting itself dates back to the 1960s–70s (Steitz used it to map bacteriophage initiation sites); Ingolia and Weissman's 2009 innovation was to combine it with deep sequencing.

items.gloss_md: Methods that measure newly synthesised RNA – i.e. active transcription by RNA polymerase – rather than steady-state RNA levels.
items.body_md:
- GRO-seq (global run-on sequencing, Core, Waterfall & Lis 2008): isolated nuclei continue transcription with labelled (Br-UTP) nucleotides, labelled RNA is pulled down and sequenced.
- PRO-seq (precision run-on, Kwak et al. 2013): biotin-NTPs stop the polymerase after one nucleotide, giving base-pair resolution of polymerase position.
- Metabolic labelling alternatives: 4sU-seq, TT-seq, SLAM-seq (4sU with chemical conversion, read as T>C mismatches).
- Applications: promoter-proximal pausing, enhancer RNAs (marking active enhancers), immediate transcriptional responses before mRNA levels change, RNA synthesis vs decay rates.

items.gloss_md: RNA-seq restricted to a predefined set of genes by amplicon PCR or hybrid capture, used for deep, cheap and robust expression or fusion analysis, mostly in clinical diagnostics.
items.body_md:
- Amplicon-based: Illumina AmpliSeq, Thermo Fisher Oncomine (Ion Torrent); anchored multiplex PCR (Archer/IDT FusionPlex) detects fusions with unknown partners.
- Capture-based: Illumina TruSight RNA Pan-Cancer, TSO 500 RNA content, Agilent SureSelect RNA panels.
- Main clinical use: gene fusion detection (NTRK1/2/3, ALK, ROS1, RET, NRG1, FGFR2), which DNA panels miss when breakpoints lie in long introns. In KRAS-wild-type PDAC, fusions such as NRG1 and NTRK are actionable (e.g. NTRK inhibitors larotrectinib/entrectinib).
- Also expression panels, splice variants (e.g. MET exon 14 skipping), works with FFPE RNA.

items.gloss_md: Sequencing of full-length transcripts (cDNA or native RNA) in single reads on PacBio or Oxford Nanopore instruments, so isoforms need not be reconstructed from short fragments.
items.body_md:
- Answers what short reads struggle with: exact isoform structures, novel transcripts, alternative transcription start/end sites, fusion transcripts, allele-specific isoforms, poly(A) tail length, and (with direct RNA) RNA modifications.
- Platforms: PacBio Iso-Seq (HiFi reads, very accurate), ONT cDNA, PCR-cDNA and direct RNA sequencing.
- Limitations: fewer reads per dollar than Illumina (lower quantitative power), library biases towards shorter transcripts, more complex analysis (tools: IsoQuant, FLAIR, SQANTI3, Bambu).
- Combined with single-cell barcodes (e.g. MAS-Seq/Kinnex single-cell) for isoform-resolved single-cell data.

items.gloss_md: PacBio's full-length cDNA sequencing method, which reads complete transcripts as highly accurate HiFi reads to catalogue isoforms.
items.body_md:
- Full-length cDNA (template-switching RT) is circularised into SMRTbell libraries and read many times (circular consensus), giving HiFi reads with ~99.9 % accuracy, typically covering whole transcripts of 1–10 kb.
- The Iso-Seq pipeline clusters reads into non-redundant isoforms; SQANTI3 classifies them against the annotation (full splice match, novel in catalogue, …).
- Kinnex (formerly MAS-Seq) concatenates several transcripts into one long molecule, raising the number of transcripts read per SMRT Cell several-fold; also for 10x single-cell libraries.
- Used for transcriptome annotation (e.g. GENCODE long-read efforts), cancer isoforms and fusion discovery.

items.gloss_md: Oxford Nanopore sequencing of native RNA molecules without reverse transcription or PCR, which reads full-length transcripts together with their chemical modifications.
items.body_md:
- A motor protein feeds the RNA 3'→5' through the pore; changes in ionic current are base-called (current RNA004 chemistry).
- Detects modifications such as m6A, pseudouridine and inosine, and measures poly(A) tail length, because native bases are read directly.
- No PCR or RT bias, but needs relatively much input RNA, gives lower throughput and accuracy than cDNA approaches, and loses the last ~10 nt at the 5' end.
- ONT also offers cDNA and PCR-cDNA kits with higher throughput for isoform quantification; nanopore sequencing of full-length 10x cDNA gives isoform-level single-cell data.
- Direct RNA sequencing was first shown in 2018 (Garalde et al., Nature Methods).

items.gloss_md: A hybridisation-based platform that counts individual RNA molecules of up to ~800 target genes using colour-coded barcode probes, without reverse transcription or amplification.
items.body_md:
- Principle: per target, a capture probe (biotinylated) and a reporter probe carrying a unique string of fluorophores hybridise in solution; complexes are immobilised and stretched in a cartridge, and the colour code of each molecule is imaged and counted digitally.
- Strengths: no enzymatic steps, so very robust with FFPE and degraded RNA; little hands-on time; highly reproducible; results in about a day; good for clinical-style assays and validation.
- Limitations: predefined panels only (up to ~800 genes; custom CodeSets possible), less dynamic range and sensitivity than RNA-seq at the low end.
- Normalisation with positive control spikes and housekeeping genes (nSolver, NanoStringNorm, RUVg).
- Clinical example: the Prosigna (PAM50) breast cancer test. Panels: PanCancer IO 360, PanCancer Immune Profiling, Banff Human Organ Transplant (B-HOT), Fibrosis, miRNA.

Introduced in 2008 (Geiss et al., Nature Biotechnology). NanoString was acquired by Bruker in 2024.

attrs.mnemonic: NanoString = 'a string of coloured beads' (the barcode) on each molecule – count the strings like a barcode scanner at the supermarket.
attrs.anecdote: The technology was invented by Krassen Dimitrov and Dwayne Dunaway at Leroy Hood's Institute for Systems Biology in Seattle, from which NanoString was spun out in 2003.

items.gloss_md: Predefined ~700–800-gene nCounter CodeSets for specific biology, such as the PanCancer IO 360 tumour–immune panel and the Banff Human Organ Transplant (B-HOT) panel.
items.body_md:
- PanCancer IO 360: 770 genes covering tumour, microenvironment and immune response, including the 18-gene Tumor Inflammation Signature (TIS) that predicts response to PD-1 blockade.
- PanCancer Immune Profiling and PanCancer Pathways: 770 genes each on immune cell types/checkpoints and on canonical cancer pathways.
- Banff Human Organ Transplant (B-HOT): 770 genes selected with the Banff Foundation for allograft pathology – rejection (T-cell-mediated and antibody-mediated), tolerance, viral infection and innate immunity; designed for FFPE biopsy molecular diagnostics in transplantation.
- Other panels: Fibrosis, Metabolic Pathways, Neuroinflammation, miRNA; custom panels and Panel Plus add-ons.

attrs.mnemonic: 770 is the magic panel size – IO 360, Immune Profiling and B-HOT all have 770 genes.

items.gloss_md: Within-sample RNA-seq expression units that correct read counts for gene (transcript) length and sequencing depth; TPM values of a sample always sum to one million.
items.body_md:
- RPKM/FPKM: reads (or fragments for paired-end) per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads – depth normalised first, then length.
- TPM: normalise for length first (reads per kb), then scale so that the sum per sample is 10^6; therefore TPM proportions are comparable between samples, which FPKM sums are not.
- Use for: comparing expression of different genes within a sample, reporting, plotting; produced by salmon, kallisto, RSEM.
- Not for differential expression: DE tools (DESeq2, edgeR, limma-voom) model raw counts with their own between-sample normalisation (median-of-ratios, TMM).
- Like all relative units, TPM is compositional: if a few genes are massively up (e.g. albumin in liver, immunoglobulins in plasma cells), all others look down.

attrs.mnemonic: TPM: 'Then Per Million' – first per length, then per million; FPKM does it the other way round.

items.label_md: Counts per million (CPM) and library-size normalisation
items.gloss_md: CPM scales raw read counts by the total number of reads in the sample (×10^6), the simplest between-sample normalisation for sequencing depth, without gene-length correction.
items.body_md:
- CPM = count / library size × 10^6; often used as log-CPM for plots, filtering lowly expressed genes (e.g. CPM > 1 in n samples) and in limma-voom.
- Library size alone is biased when a few highly expressed genes dominate (composition effects); robust size factors fix this:
  - TMM (trimmed mean of M-values, edgeR, Robinson & Oshlack 2010),
  - median-of-ratios (DESeq2), which assumes most genes are not differentially expressed.
- Single-cell analogue: total-count normalisation to 10,000 (Seurat "LogNormalize", Scanpy normalize_total), or scran pooling and sctransform.

items.gloss_md: Synthetic RNA molecules of known sequence and concentration added to samples to calibrate and quality-control RNA measurements.
items.body_md:
- ERCC (External RNA Controls Consortium) mix: 92 synthetic polyadenylated transcripts spanning ~10^6-fold concentration range; Mix 1/Mix 2 with known fold changes test accuracy of DE.
- Lexogen SIRVs (spike-in RNA variants) test isoform quantification; Sequins mimic human genes.
- Uses: sensitivity and dynamic range, detection of global expression shifts (which standard normalisation hides), absolute scale in single-cell (e.g. Smart-seq2) experiments.
- Limitations: spike-ins differ from endogenous RNA (no cap, short poly(A), different structure) and must be added in accurately equal amounts per cell or per RNA.

items.gloss_md: Classic method in which RNA is separated by size on a denaturing gel, transferred to a membrane and detected with a labelled probe, showing transcript size and abundance.
items.body_md:
- Steps: denaturing agarose (formaldehyde) or polyacrylamide gel → transfer (blotting) to nylon → UV crosslink → hybridisation with a radioactive or chemiluminescent probe.
- Shows transcript size and isoforms directly; still used for small RNAs and to validate novel transcripts.
- Low throughput and sensitivity; replaced by RT-qPCR and RNA-seq for routine use.

Introduced by Alwine, Kemp and Stark in 1977.

attrs.mnemonic: SNOW DROP: Southern – DNA, Northern – RNA, Western – Protein.
attrs.anecdote: Only the Southern blot is named after a person (Edwin Southern, 1975); Northern and Western are jokes playing on his name, and the Eastern blot never settled on one meaning.

items.gloss_md: Sequencing of the 5' ends of capped RNAs to map transcription start sites and promoter activity genome-wide.
items.body_md:
- The 5' cap is chemically biotinylated and captured ("cap-trapping"); a short tag from the 5' end is sequenced and counted.
- Gives transcription start sites at base-pair resolution, quantifies promoter usage and alternative promoters, and detects enhancer RNAs (bidirectional transcription).
- Developed at RIKEN (Japan); the basis of the FANTOM5 atlas of promoters and enhancers across human cell types.
- Single-cell 5' methods (10x 5', C1 CAGE) capture similar information.

items.gloss_md: Systematic technical differences between groups of samples processed separately (different day, kit lot, operator, run, site) that are unrelated to biology but can dominate or mimic biological signals.
items.body_md:
- Sources: RNA extraction and library batches, sequencing runs/flow cells, array scan dates, reagent lots, tissue handling time, hospitals in multi-centre studies; in single-cell data each sample/channel is its own batch.
- Detection: PCA/UMAP coloured by batch, hierarchical clustering, control samples run in every batch.
- Prevention is better than correction: randomise or block samples across batches, never confound batch with the condition (if all cirrhosis samples are in batch 1 and all controls in batch 2, the effect cannot be separated).
- Correction: include batch as a covariate in the model (DESeq2, limma); ComBat/ComBat-seq (Johnson et al. 2007); limma removeBatchEffect for visualisation; RUV with control genes; single-cell integration methods (Harmony, Seurat anchors, scVI).
- Over-correction can remove real biology when batch and biology are partly confounded.

attrs.mnemonic: A batch effect is like comparing photos taken with different cameras: you must first know which camera took which picture.
attrs.anecdote: Leek et al. (Nature Reviews Genetics, 2010) showed that processing date alone explained a large share of the variation in several landmark high-throughput data sets, making 'batch effects' a mainstream concern.

items.gloss_md: Sequencing depth is the number of reads per sample (or coverage per base, per cell); saturation describes how close the sampled reads are to having observed every molecule in the library.
items.body_md:
- Bulk RNA-seq: ~20–30 million reads per sample for gene-level DE, more (50–100 M) for isoforms, splicing or low-expressed genes; 3' tag methods ~2–10 M.
- DNA sequencing: expressed as mean coverage (×): WGS ~30× germline, tumours 60–100×; exomes ~100×; targeted panels 500–1,000×+ (ctDNA panels much deeper) to see low-frequency variants.
- Single-cell: reads per cell (10x recommends ≥ ~20,000 read pairs per cell for 3' gene expression); sequencing saturation = 1 − (unique UMIs / reads); extra reads at high saturation mostly re-read the same molecules.
- More biological replicates usually buy more statistical power than more depth per sample.
- Saturation (rarefaction) curves help decide whether deeper sequencing would add genes/molecules.

attrs.mnemonic: Depth is a fishing trip: the first hours bring many new fish, later you keep catching the same ones again – that's saturation.

items.gloss_md: Massively parallel DNA sequencing in which millions to billions of DNA fragments are sequenced simultaneously, in contrast to one-fragment-at-a-time Sanger sequencing.
items.body_md:
- Also called high-throughput or second-generation sequencing (short reads, mainly Illumina); "third-generation" refers to single-molecule long-read technologies (PacBio, Oxford Nanopore).
- Common workflow: library preparation (fragmentation, adapters, indexes) → clonal amplification on a surface (clusters, beads, nanoballs) → cyclic sequencing chemistry and detection → base calling → FASTQ files.
- Applications: whole-genome, exome and panel sequencing; RNA-seq; ChIP-/ATAC-seq; methylation; single-cell and spatial methods; metagenomics; liquid biopsy (ctDNA, donor-derived cell-free DNA).
- Cost per human genome dropped from ~US$100 million (2001) to a few hundred dollars today, faster than Moore's law.

First commercial NGS instrument: 454 pyrosequencing (2005); Solexa/Illumina Genome Analyzer (2006).

attrs.anecdote: The Human Genome Project (finished 2003) cost about US$3 billion with Sanger sequencing; NHGRI's cost-per-genome chart shows the price falling off Moore's-law pace after NGS arrived in 2007–2008.

items.gloss_md: The dominant short-read sequencing chemistry: clonal clusters on a flow cell are extended one fluorescently labelled reversible-terminator nucleotide per cycle, and each cycle is imaged to read the base.
items.body_md:
- Cluster generation: adapter-ligated fragments bind to oligos on the flow cell and are amplified by bridge amplification (or ExAmp on patterned flow cells) into clusters of identical copies.
- Each cycle: add all four labelled, 3'-blocked nucleotides → image → cleave dye and blocker → next cycle; so reads have a fixed length (typically 50–300 cycles, commonly 2×150 bp paired-end).
- Detection: 4-colour (MiSeq, older HiSeq) or 2-colour (NextSeq, NovaSeq 6000; dark = G, so failed clusters produce poly-G tails); XLEAP-SBS chemistry on NovaSeq X.
- Accuracy: error rate ~0.1–1 %, mostly substitutions, quality declines along the read; >80 % of bases ≥ Q30 typical.
- Issues: index hopping on patterned flow cells (use unique dual indexes), GC bias, phasing.

Developed by Solexa (Balasubramanian and Klenerman, Cambridge), acquired by Illumina in 2007.

attrs.mnemonic: SBS = one Step, one Base, one Snapshot per cycle.
attrs.anecdote: Shankar Balasubramanian and David Klenerman reportedly conceived the approach in a Cambridge pub in the late 1990s; Solexa was later bought by Illumina, and both received the 2020 Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences for it.

items.gloss_md: Illumina's production-scale sequencers that produce billions of reads per run and are used by core facilities for large RNA-seq, single-cell, exome and genome projects.
items.body_md:
- NovaSeq 6000 (2017): patterned flow cells SP, S1, S2, S4; 2-colour SBS; up to several billion read pairs per S4 flow cell; standard for 10x single-cell and population genomics.
- NovaSeq X and X Plus (launched 2022/2023): XLEAP-SBS chemistry, higher density flow cells (1.5B, 10B, 25B), lower cost per genome, on-board DRAGEN secondary analysis.
- Typical use in a university hospital: core facility runs where many projects share lanes; read configurations like 2×150 bp or 28/90 for 10x.

items.gloss_md: Illumina's mid-throughput benchtop sequencers, used by individual labs and small cores for RNA-seq, panels and modest single-cell projects.
items.body_md:
- NextSeq 500/550 (2014): first 2-colour SBS instrument; high- and mid-output kits with up to ~400 million single reads; the 550 can also scan BeadChip arrays.
- NextSeq 1000/2000 (2020): P1–P4 flow cells, up to around a billion+ reads per run on the 2000, on-board DRAGEN.
- Sits between MiSeq (small) and NovaSeq (production scale).
- Typical jobs: bulk RNA-seq batches of 24–96 samples, targeted panels, ATAC/ChIP, small 10x projects; run times about 1–2 days.

items.gloss_md: Illumina's small benchtop sequencer with the longest Illumina reads (2×300 bp) but low output (~tens of millions of reads), used for amplicons, small panels, microbes and library QC.
items.body_md:
- Up to 2×300 bp paired-end, ~25 million reads per v3 run; 4-colour SBS.
- Uses: 16S rRNA amplicon microbiome sequencing, small targeted panels, bacterial/viral genomes, CRISPR edit checking, test runs to balance pooled libraries before NovaSeq.
- MiSeqDx is FDA-cleared for clinical assays; succeeded by the MiSeq i100 series (2024). Smaller still: iSeq 100.
- Reads per run are too few for most RNA-seq or single-cell projects, so it is a QC and small-target instrument rather than a workhorse.

items.gloss_md: Sequencing both ends of each DNA fragment (read 1 and read 2), which gives two linked reads with a known approximate distance (insert size).
items.body_md:
- Notation: 2×150 bp means 150 cycles for read 1 and read 2; index reads (i7, i5) are read separately.
- Benefits: better mapping in repeats, detection of structural variants and gene fusions (discordant pairs, split reads), isoform resolution, accurate duplicate identification.
- Single-end reads (e.g. 1×75) are cheaper and sufficient for simple counting (3' tag RNA-seq, ChIP-seq).
- In 10x single-cell libraries the pair is asymmetric: read 1 (28 bp) holds cell barcode + UMI, read 2 holds the cDNA.
- Mate-pair libraries (large inserts of several kb) are a different, now rare, design.

items.gloss_md: The standard text format for raw sequencing reads, storing each read's identifier, sequence and per-base quality scores in four lines.
items.body_md:
Four lines per read:
1. @read identifier (instrument, run, flow cell, lane, tile, coordinates, read number, index),
2. the sequence,
3. a "+" separator,
4. the quality string, one ASCII character per base (Phred+33: Q = ASCII code − 33).

- Paired-end data come as _R1/_R2 files (plus _I1/_I2 index reads, needed e.g. for 10x); usually gzip-compressed (.fastq.gz).
- Produced from Illumina BCL files by bcl2fastq/BCL Convert (demultiplexing); first QC with FastQC/MultiQC, trimming with cutadapt/fastp.

attrs.mnemonic: FASTQ = FASTA + Quality.

items.gloss_md: A logarithmic measure of base-calling accuracy: Q = −10·log10(P_error), so Q20 means 1 error in 100 and Q30 means 1 error in 1,000 bases.
items.body_md:
- Q10 = 90 %, Q20 = 99 %, Q30 = 99.9 %, Q40 = 99.99 % accuracy.
- Illumina run specs are given as % bases ≥ Q30; PacBio HiFi reads are typically ≥ Q20–Q30; "Q40+" is marketed by Element and newer platforms.
- Encoded in FASTQ as ASCII characters (offset 33).
- Named after the Phred base-calling program (Ewing & Green, 1998) from the Human Genome Project era.

attrs.mnemonic: Every 10 Q points add one 'nine': Q20 = 99 %, Q30 = 99.9 %, Q40 = 99.99 %.

items.gloss_md: Adding short sample-specific index (barcode) sequences to libraries so that many samples can be pooled and sequenced together and later separated computationally.
items.body_md:
- Illumina libraries carry an i7 and (dual indexing) an i5 index read in separate index reads; demultiplexing with bcl2fastq/BCL Convert assigns reads to samples via a sample sheet.
- Unique dual indexes (UDIs) protect against index hopping (free adapters swapping reads between samples, especially on patterned flow cells) and against index read errors.
- Pools must be balanced (molarity measured by qPCR/Qubit/Bioanalyzer) so each sample gets its share of reads.
- Not to be confused with cell barcodes (single-cell) or UMIs, which are inside the read structure, though the principle – a tag that identifies origin – is the same.

items.gloss_md: Conversion of a DNA or RNA sample into a pool of fragments with platform-specific adapters (and indexes) that can be sequenced.
items.body_md:
- Typical DNA steps: fragmentation (sonication, enzymatic or Tn5 tagmentation) → end repair and A-tailing → adapter ligation → optional PCR → size selection/cleanup → QC (Qubit, Bioanalyzer/TapeStation, qPCR).
- RNA-seq adds RNA selection (poly(A) or rRNA depletion), fragmentation and reverse transcription; stranded kits mark the second strand.
- Enrichment variants: hybrid capture (exome, panels), amplicon PCR, immunoprecipitation (ChIP), Tn5 on chromatin (ATAC).
- Artefacts introduced here: PCR duplicates, GC bias, adapter dimers, chimeras; UMIs and PCR-free protocols reduce some.
- Tagmentation (Nextera/Illumina DNA Prep) combines fragmentation and adapter addition in one step using Tn5 transposase.

attrs.mnemonic: Library prep = putting a 'handle' (adapter) on every fragment so the sequencer can grab it.

items.gloss_md: Chain-termination DNA sequencing: DNA polymerase randomly incorporates fluorescent dideoxynucleotides that stop extension, and capillary electrophoresis reads the sequence of a single ~800-bp fragment.
items.body_md:
- Reads up to ~800–1,000 bp with very high accuracy per base; one fragment (one amplicon) per reaction.
- Still the gold standard to confirm individual variants found by NGS, check plasmids and CRISPR edits, and for HLA or single-gene diagnostics.
- Limitation in cancer: detects variants only above ~15–20 % allele fraction, so low-cellularity tumours like PDAC (often <20–30 % tumour cells) need NGS or digital PCR for KRAS testing.
- Instruments: Applied Biosystems 3500/3730 capillary sequencers.

Published by Frederick Sanger in 1977.

attrs.anecdote: Frederick Sanger won two Nobel Prizes in Chemistry: 1958 for the structure (sequence) of insulin and 1980 for DNA sequencing.

items.gloss_md: Sequencing of the complete genome of a sample, detecting single-nucleotide variants, indels, copy-number and structural variants in coding and non-coding regions.
items.body_md:
- Short-read WGS at ~30× (germline) or ~60–100× tumour plus matched normal (somatic); PCR-free libraries reduce GC bias.
- Detects everything at once: SNVs/indels, CNVs, structural variants and rearrangements, mutational signatures, tumour mutational burden, HRD scores; genome-wide signatures (e.g. in PDAC, the "unstable" genome subtype with BRCA-like signature).
- Low-pass WGS (~0.1–1×) is enough for copy-number profiling, including cfDNA.
- Long-read WGS (PacBio HiFi, ONT) resolves repeats, phasing and complex SVs.
- Larger datasets and more variants of unknown significance than exome or panels; increasingly used in rare disease and cancer diagnostics.

attrs.mnemonic: Genome > exome > panel: the wider the net, the shallower the depth (WGS ~30×, WES ~100×, panels 500×+).

items.gloss_md: Sequencing of all protein-coding exons (~1–2 % of the genome, ~20,000 genes) after hybrid-capture enrichment, as a cheaper alternative to whole-genome sequencing.
items.body_md:
- Capture kits (e.g. Agilent SureSelect, IDT xGen, Twist) target ~35–60 Mb; typical mean coverage ~100× (higher for tumours).
- Finds most known pathogenic germline variants and somatic coding mutations; used in rare-disease diagnostics and cancer genomics (e.g. TCGA).
- Limitations: uneven coverage, misses non-coding and most structural variants, less reliable copy-number calling than WGS.
- Tumour–normal exome pairs give somatic mutations and tumour mutational burden (TMB).

attrs.mnemonic: Exome = the ~1–2 % of the genome that 'exits' as protein.

items.gloss_md: NGS of a selected set of genes (tens to hundreds) by hybrid capture or amplicon PCR at high depth, the standard for clinical tumour and hereditary-cancer testing.
items.body_md:
- High coverage (often 500–1,000×+) detects variants at low allele fractions in low-cellularity samples (FFPE biopsies, PDAC) and ctDNA.
- Examples: FoundationOne CDx (324 genes), Illumina TruSight Oncology 500 (523 genes, also TMB and MSI), Oncomine (Ion Torrent), hereditary cancer panels (BRCA1/2, PALB2, ATM, mismatch-repair genes).
- In PDAC: KRAS status, rarer actionable alterations (BRAF, NTRK/NRG1 fusions via RNA, MSI-high/dMMR) and germline BRCA1/2/PALB2 (olaparib maintenance after the POLO trial; platinum sensitivity).
- Results are discussed in molecular tumour boards; variants are classified for actionability (e.g. ESCAT, OncoKB levels).

items.gloss_md: Single-molecule sequencing that produces reads of thousands to millions of bases (PacBio, Oxford Nanopore), often called third-generation sequencing.
items.body_md:
- Two main technologies: PacBio SMRT (HiFi reads ~15–25 kb, ~99.9 % accurate) and Oxford Nanopore (reads from hundreds of bases to >1 Mb, accuracy improved to ~99 %+ with current chemistry).
- Strengths: repeats, segmental duplications and structural variants, haplotype phasing, telomere-to-telomere assemblies (the T2T-CHM13 human genome, 2022), full-length transcripts, direct detection of DNA/RNA modifications (5mC) without bisulfite.
- Limitations: more DNA input (high molecular weight), lower throughput per dollar than Illumina for counting applications.
- Short reads remain standard for expression counting and most clinical panels.

attrs.anecdote: The first truly complete (gapless, telomere-to-telomere) human genome, T2T-CHM13, was only finished in 2022 – nearly 20 years after the 'finished' Human Genome Project – thanks to PacBio HiFi and ultra-long nanopore reads.

items.gloss_md: Pacific Biosciences' single-molecule real-time sequencing, in which circularised DNA is read many times by one polymerase in a zero-mode waveguide to produce long (~15–25 kb), highly accurate HiFi reads.
items.body_md:
- SMRT: a single polymerase sits at the bottom of a zero-mode waveguide (ZMW) nanowell; incorporation of fluorescent nucleotides is recorded in real time.
- HiFi (circular consensus sequencing, CCS): the circular SMRTbell template is read repeatedly; the consensus reaches Q30+ (≥99.9 %).
- Kinetics of incorporation reveal base modifications (5mC in CpG) without bisulfite.
- Instruments: Sequel II/IIe, Revio (2023, high throughput), Vega (benchtop).
- Uses: genome assembly, structural variants, phasing, Iso-Seq full-length transcripts, HLA typing, repeat expansions. PacBio also sells Onso, a short-read instrument.

attrs.mnemonic: HiFi = read the same circle again and again until the 'record' plays perfectly.

items.gloss_md: Sequencing in which single DNA or RNA strands are pulled through protein nanopores in a membrane and the changes in ionic current are decoded into bases in real time.
items.body_md:
- A motor protein ratchets the strand through the pore; neural-network basecallers (Dorado) translate the current signal; reads range from hundreds of bases to >1 Mb (ultra-long).
- Devices: Flongle and MinION (USB-sized, portable), GridION, PromethION (high throughput).
- Strengths: longest reads, real-time analysis and adaptive sampling (reject unwanted molecules on the fly), direct RNA and native base modification detection (5mC, 5hmC, m6A), low capital cost, field use (Ebola, SARS-CoV-2 surveillance).
- Accuracy: historically ~85–95 %; with R10.4.1 pores and current basecallers typically ≥ Q20 (99 %), with remaining homopolymer errors.
- Clinical research: rapid intraoperative brain tumour methylation classification, structural variants, pathogen identification.

attrs.mnemonic: Nanopore = reading a necklace by feeling each bead as it slips through your fingers.
attrs.anecdote: A MinION was used aboard the International Space Station in 2016 – the first DNA sequencing in space.

items.gloss_md: Thermo Fisher's short-read sequencing technology that detects nucleotide incorporation through the release of hydrogen ions (a pH change) on a semiconductor chip, without optics.
items.body_md:
- Template DNA on beads (emulsion PCR or isothermal amplification) sits in millions of microwells over ion sensors; nucleotides are flowed one type at a time and each incorporation releases H+.
- Fast runs and simple instruments (Ion GeneStudio S5, Genexus integrated sample-to-report system); reads ~200–600 bp.
- Weakness: homopolymer runs (e.g. AAAAA) produce indel errors because signal size must be counted.
- Main niche: clinical amplicon panels (Oncomine Dx Target Test, Oncomine Comprehensive/Precision assays) with low DNA input from FFPE.

Introduced in 2010 by Jonathan Rothberg's company Ion Torrent, acquired by Life Technologies (now Thermo Fisher).

attrs.mnemonic: Ion Torrent = 'pH-meter sequencing': every incorporated base makes the well a little more acidic.

items.gloss_md: Short-read sequencing platform from MGI Tech (BGI group) that amplifies circular DNA into DNA nanoballs by rolling-circle amplification and reads them with combinatorial probe-anchor synthesis.
items.body_md:
- Rolling-circle amplification yields nanoballs (copies of one template, linear amplification, so fewer PCR errors and duplicates); DNBs are loaded on patterned arrays.
- Chemistry: cPAS (combinatorial probe-anchor synthesis), fluorescent reversible terminators similar in concept to Illumina SBS.
- Instruments: DNBSEQ-G99, -G400, -T7, -T20 (very high throughput); typically lower cost per Gb; low index hopping.
- Output quality is comparable to Illumina for RNA-seq and WGS; the same DNB technology underlies Stereo-seq spatial transcriptomics. Availability in some markets is affected by regulatory and political issues.

items.gloss_md: Benchtop short-read sequencer launched in 2022 that uses avidity sequencing – multivalent nucleotide–polymer conjugates – to achieve very high base accuracy at low cost.
items.body_md:
- Avidity chemistry separates stepping (unlabelled reversible terminators) from detection (fluorescent multivalent "avidites" that bind the template strongly at low concentration).
- Reads up to 2×150/2×300 bp; high fraction of bases above Q40; lower cost per Gb than comparable Illumina benchtops.
- Also offers AVITI24 for in-sample (cytoprofiling) readouts of RNA and protein in cells.
- Described in Arslan et al., Nature Biotechnology 2023.

items.gloss_md: RNA sequencing of individual cells, in which each cell's transcripts are tagged with a cell barcode so that thousands to millions of cells can be profiled and cell types and states resolved.
items.body_md:
- Workflow: tissue dissociation → single-cell suspension → isolation (droplets, wells, plates or combinatorial indexing) → lysis and reverse transcription with cell barcodes and UMIs → amplification → library → sequencing → cell × gene count matrix.
- Families: droplet (10x Chromium, Drop-seq, inDrops), plate-based full-length (Smart-seq2/3), plate 3' (CEL-seq2, MARS-seq), microwell (BD Rhapsody, Seq-Well), combinatorial indexing (sci-RNA-seq, SPLiT-seq/Parse); nuclei instead of cells (snRNA-seq).
- Typical analysis: QC (genes/UMIs per cell, % mitochondrial reads, doublets, ambient RNA) → normalisation → highly variable genes → PCA → integration → clustering and UMAP → marker-based annotation → differential expression (pseudobulk), trajectories (pseudotime, RNA velocity), cell–cell communication (CellChat, NicheNet). Tools: Seurat (R), Scanpy (Python).
- Strengths: reveals cell heterogeneity, rare populations, tumour microenvironment, immune states; atlases such as the Human Cell Atlas.
- Limitations: sparse data and dropout, dissociation bias (fragile cells lost, stress genes), loss of spatial context, cost per sample, need for biological replicates (patients, not cells, are the unit of replication).

First single-cell transcriptome by sequencing: Tang et al. 2009 (Surani lab).

attrs.mnemonic: Bulk RNA-seq is a fruit smoothie, scRNA-seq is a fruit salad: same fruits, but now you can see each piece.
attrs.anecdote: Single-cell sequencing was Nature Methods' 'Method of the Year' 2013, and the 2009 study by Tang et al. sequenced just one mouse blastomere at a time – today a single 10x run profiles tens of thousands of cells.

items.label_md: 10x Genomics Chromium Single Cell 3' Gene Expression
items.gloss_md: The most widely used scRNA-seq platform: a microfluidic chip co-encapsulates single cells with barcoded gel beads in oil droplets (GEMs), where poly(A) RNA is reverse-transcribed with a cell barcode and UMI, and 3' ends are sequenced.
items.body_md:
- Gel bead oligo: Illumina read 1 primer – 16-nt 10x cell barcode – 12-nt UMI (v3) – 30-nt poly(dT). Read 1 (28 bp) = barcode + UMI, read 2 (~90 bp) = cDNA near the 3' end.
- Throughput: typically 500–10,000 cells recovered per channel (up to ~20,000 with HT/GEM-X kits), 8 channels per chip; cell recovery ~50–65 % of loaded cells.
- Multiplet rate rises with loading (~0.8 % per 1,000 recovered cells for v3.1).
- Chemistry versions: v2 (2017), v3/v3.1 (2018/2020), GEM-X / v4 (2024, higher sensitivity, lower multiplets). Instruments: Chromium Controller, Chromium X / iX.
- Typical sensitivity: a few thousand genes and several thousand UMIs per cell, depending on cell type.
- Processing with Cell Ranger, then Seurat/Scanpy; Feature Barcode add-ons capture CITE-seq antibodies, cell hashing and CRISPR guides.
- Limitations: 3' end only (no isoforms or full-length), needs fresh viable single-cell suspensions (or nuclei; fixed cells via Flex), cost per sample.

Described in Zheng et al., Nature Communications 2017; commercial since 2016.

attrs.mnemonic: 10x read 1 = '16 + 12 = 28': 16 for the cell, 12 for the molecule (UMI) – who and which.
attrs.anecdote: 10x Genomics started (2012) with droplet-based linked-read DNA sequencing for long-range genome information; that product was discontinued in 2020, while the single-cell application built on the same droplet chips made the company.

items.gloss_md: 10x Genomics' 5' scRNA-seq assay, in which the cell barcode is added by template switching at the 5' end of transcripts, allowing paired TCR/BCR (V(D)J) sequencing from the same cells.
items.body_md:
- The barcode and UMI sit on the template-switch oligo, so libraries capture the 5' end; the full-length cDNA is also used to enrich V(D)J regions of T-cell and B-cell receptors.
- From one sample: 5' gene expression + TCR (α/β chains) + BCR (heavy/light chains) + optional Feature Barcode surface protein (TotalSeq-C) and antigen specificity (dCODE dextramers).
- Clonotypes link clonal expansion to phenotype (e.g. tumour-reactive CD8 T cells, alloreactive T cells in rejection biopsies, plasmablasts).
- Gene expression quality is comparable to the 3' assay; both are analysed with Cell Ranger (multi).

attrs.mnemonic: Receptors are read from the 5' end: 'five for the front' – V(D)J sits at the front of the transcript.

items.gloss_md: The nanolitre oil droplet in 10x Genomics microfluidics that contains one barcoded gel bead, at most (ideally) one cell, and reverse-transcription reagents.
items.body_md:
- In the chip, gel beads, cells with RT mix, and partitioning oil meet at a junction; the bead dissolves and releases millions of copies of one barcode oligo.
- Cells are loaded at limiting dilution (Poisson), so most GEMs contain no cell, some one, and a few two or more (multiplets); bead loading is nearly 100 %.
- Inside each GEM, RNA is captured and reverse-transcribed; then the emulsion is broken and all barcoded cDNA is pooled.
- Empty GEMs still contain ambient RNA – the origin of the "soup" that cell-calling algorithms must distinguish from real cells.

items.gloss_md: A short DNA sequence attached to all cDNA molecules from one cell (or droplet/well), allowing reads from thousands of pooled cells to be assigned back to their cell of origin.
items.body_md:
- Delivered by beads (10x: 16-nt barcodes from a whitelist of roughly 0.7–7 million, depending on chemistry), well-specific primers (plates) or several ligation rounds (combinatorial indexing: barcode = combination of round barcodes).
- Processing: match to the whitelist allowing one mismatch, then "cell calling" separates real cells from empty droplets (knee plot, EmptyDrops).
- Collisions: two cells sharing a barcode (doublets) or one cell split across barcodes are possible but rare.
- Different from the sample index (identifies the library) and from the UMI (identifies the molecule).

attrs.mnemonic: Three tags, three questions: sample index = which tube, cell barcode = which cell, UMI = which molecule.

items.gloss_md: A random oligonucleotide tag (typically 8–12 nt) attached to each original molecule before PCR, so that amplified copies can be collapsed and molecules, not reads, are counted.
items.body_md:
- Reads with the same cell barcode, gene and UMI derive from one original cDNA molecule; collapsing them removes PCR amplification bias and duplicates.
- Count matrices of droplet scRNA-seq are therefore UMI counts (approximately molecule counts).
- Errors in UMIs (sequencing or PCR errors) inflate counts; tools such as UMI-tools and Cell Ranger merge UMIs within one mismatch.
- Also used in bulk: 3' tag and BRB-seq, and in ultra-deep ctDNA panels where UMI consensus reads suppress sequencing errors so very-low-frequency mutations can be called.
- Full-length Smart-seq2 has no UMIs (reads, not molecules); Smart-seq3 added them.

Introduced around 2011–2012 (Kivioja et al., "Counting absolute numbers of molecules using unique molecular identifiers").

attrs.mnemonic: UMI = a name tag on each guest before the party (PCR): however many photos (reads) you take, you count each named guest once.

items.gloss_md: The ways single cells are separated for single-cell sequencing: FACS into plates, microfluidic droplets, microwells, valve-based chips, or no physical separation at all (combinatorial indexing).
items.body_md:
- FACS into 96/384-well plates: select cells by surface markers, index sorting records each cell's fluorescence; low throughput, high sensitivity (Smart-seq2, MARS-seq).
- Droplet microfluidics: thousands of cells per run, little selection (10x Chromium, Drop-seq, inDrops).
- Microwells: cells settle by gravity into wells with barcoded beads (BD Rhapsody, Seq-Well).
- Integrated fluidic circuits: Fluidigm (Standard BioTools) C1, historic, ~96–800 cells.
- Combinatorial indexing: fixed cells/nuclei stay in pools while barcodes are added in rounds (sci-RNA-seq, Parse Evercode, Scale Bio).
- Others: micromanipulation, laser capture microdissection, image-based dispensing (cellenONE).
- Upstream step common to all: dissociation into a viable single-cell suspension or nuclei isolation.

items.gloss_md: A barcode that contains RNA from two (or more) cells, appearing as an artificial 'hybrid' cell expressing markers of both.
items.body_md:
- Arises when two cells land in one droplet/well or stick together; the rate grows with the number of loaded cells (≈ linearly in droplet systems).
- Heterotypic doublets (different cell types) can masquerade as novel transitional cell states, e.g. "T cell–macrophage" clusters; homotypic doublets are mainly larger counts and hard to detect.
- Detection: computational (Scrublet, DoubletFinder, scDblFinder – simulate artificial doublets and score similarity), sample multiplexing (cross-sample doublets from cell hashing or genotype), unusually high UMI counts.
- Removing doublets before clustering is a standard QC step.

attrs.mnemonic: A doublet looks like a 'chimera' cell – if a cluster expresses CD3E and LYZ at the same time, suspect two cells, not a new cell type.

items.gloss_md: Cell-free RNA from lysed or damaged cells in the cell suspension that is captured in droplets along with intact cells, contaminating every cell's profile with a background 'soup' of transcripts.
items.body_md:
- Typical signs: highly expressed transcripts of an abundant or fragile cell type appear at low levels in all clusters – e.g. albumin and other hepatocyte genes everywhere in liver data, haemoglobin genes from red blood cells, PRSS1/CPA1/CELA3A from acinar cells in pancreas and PDAC samples.
- Especially strong in single-nucleus data and in tissues with fragile or lysis-prone cells.
- Correction: SoupX (estimates the soup from empty droplets), CellBender (deep generative model, also improves cell calling), DecontX.
- Prevention: good dissociation, dead-cell removal, washing, avoid long handling.

attrs.mnemonic: Ambient RNA = the soup in which all the cells swim – every droplet gets a spoonful.

items.gloss_md: The phenomenon that a gene expressed in a cell is not detected (zero count) because only a fraction of each cell's mRNA molecules is captured and sequenced.
items.body_md:
- Causes: limited capture and RT efficiency (only a minority of mRNAs per cell end up as UMIs), sampling at finite sequencing depth, low-abundance transcripts.
- Consequence: count matrices are mostly zeros (often >90 %), single marker genes are unreliable per cell; prefer cluster-level or signature-level statements.
- Debate: UMI-based droplet data are largely consistent with negative-binomial sampling without extra "zero inflation" (Svensson 2020); plate-based read counts show more excess zeros.
- Remedies: aggregate cells (pseudobulk, metacells), use gene modules, careful imputation (MAGIC, ALRA) only for visualisation, deeper sequencing, more sensitive chemistries.

attrs.mnemonic: A zero in single-cell data means 'not seen', not 'not there'.

items.gloss_md: The percentage of a cell's reads or UMIs from mitochondrially encoded genes (MT- genes), used as a quality metric: high values indicate damaged or dying cells that have lost cytoplasmic mRNA.
items.body_md:
- Common thresholds: 5–20 % depending on tissue and protocol; must be tissue-aware – hepatocytes, cardiomyocytes and kidney tubule cells are mitochondria-rich and naturally high, so strict cut-offs remove them.
- Combined with number of genes/UMIs per cell (very low = empty droplet or debris, very high = doublet).
- In single-nucleus data, mitochondrial reads should be near zero; high values indicate cytoplasmic contamination.
- Genes are named "MT-…" in human (e.g. MT-CO1, MT-ND1) and "mt-…" in mouse, which is how the percentage is computed.

attrs.mnemonic: Leaky cell, leaky RNA: when the membrane breaks, cytoplasmic mRNA escapes but mitochondria (with their RNA) stay inside – so the mito percentage goes up.

items.gloss_md: Biases introduced when tissue is enzymatically and mechanically dissociated for single-cell sequencing: stress-gene induction and loss or under-representation of fragile cell types.
items.body_md:
- Enzymatic digestion at 37 °C induces immediate-early and heat-shock genes (FOS, JUN, EGR1, HSPA1A/B) within minutes (van den Brink et al. 2017) – a "dissociation signature" that can be mistaken for biology.
- Cell-type bias: hepatocytes (large, fragile), neurons, adipocytes, neutrophils and acinar cells are lost or damaged; robust immune and stromal cells are over-represented.
- Countermeasures: cold-active proteases at 4–6 °C, transcription inhibitors (actinomycin D) during dissociation, fixation (10x Flex, ACME), single-nucleus RNA-seq on frozen tissue, or spatial methods.
- Relevant to liver (hepatocyte loss) and pancreas (autodigestion by acinar enzymes).

items.gloss_md: 10x Genomics' official software that turns Chromium sequencing data into cell-by-feature count matrices (and V(D)J contigs) by barcode processing, STAR alignment, UMI counting and cell calling.
items.body_md:
- Main commands: cellranger count (one gene-expression library), multi (GEX + V(D)J + Feature Barcode + multiplexing), aggr (combine samples), vdj; mkfastq is replaced by BCL Convert.
- Outputs: filtered_feature_bc_matrix (MTX + barcodes + features; or .h5), raw matrix including empty droplets, BAM, web_summary.html with QC (estimated cells, median genes per cell, sequencing saturation, % reads in cells), Loupe Browser file (.cloupe).
- Since version 7 intronic reads are counted by default (include-introns), suiting nuclei.
- Free alternatives: STARsolo, alevin-fry (simpleaf), kallisto | bustools. Siblings: Space Ranger (Visium), Xenium Ranger, Cell Ranger ARC (Multiome).

items.gloss_md: A plate-based single-cell method that produces full-length cDNA by oligo-dT priming and template switching, giving high sensitivity and coverage of entire transcripts for hundreds of cells.
items.body_md:
- Cells are sorted (FACS) into 96/384-well plates; SMART = switching mechanism at the 5' end of the RNA template: the reverse transcriptase adds extra Cs, a template-switch oligo binds and the full transcript is copied.
- Full-length cDNA is amplified by PCR and tagmented (Tn5, Nextera) – reads cover the whole transcript.
- Strengths: detects more genes per cell than droplet methods, isoforms and splicing, SNVs and allele-specific expression, reconstruction of TCR sequences (TraCeR), index-sorting data links protein markers to transcriptome.
- Limitations: no UMIs (read counts, PCR bias), low throughput, higher cost per cell, separate library per cell.

Picelli et al., Nature Methods 2013 (Sandberg lab).

attrs.mnemonic: SMART = Switching Mechanism At 5' end of RNA Template.

items.gloss_md: Improved full-length plate-based scRNA-seq that adds a 5' UMI to the Smart-seq chemistry, combining molecule counting with full-transcript coverage.
items.body_md:
- A tagged template-switch oligo with an 8-nt UMI marks the 5' ends; 5' reads are counted as molecules, internal reads reconstruct isoforms and allelic transcripts.
- Higher sensitivity than Smart-seq2; miniaturised and cheaper version Smart-seq3xpress (2022) increases throughput.
- Commercial relatives: Takara SMART-Seq kits (e.g. SMART-Seq Pro, SMART-Seq mRNA).

Hagemann-Jensen et al., Nature Biotechnology 2020 (Sandberg lab).
- Like Smart-seq2, cells are sorted into plates, so throughput is hundreds to a few thousand cells; it is chosen when isoforms, allele-specific expression or deep per-cell profiles matter more than cell numbers.

items.gloss_md: Plate-based 3' scRNA-seq that barcodes each cell's cDNA during reverse transcription, pools early and amplifies linearly by in vitro transcription, with UMIs.
items.body_md:
- CEL-seq = cell expression by linear amplification and sequencing (Hashimshony et al. 2012); CEL-seq2 (2016) added UMIs and improved sensitivity.
- Early pooling after barcoded RT reduces hands-on cost; IVT linear amplification avoids exponential PCR bias.
- Used in plate-based workflows such as SORT-seq; inDrops also uses CEL-seq-style chemistry.
- Being 3'-tagged and UMI-based, it counts molecules rather than reads, but gives no full-length isoform information; throughput is limited to plates of 96–384 cells per batch.

items.gloss_md: Massively parallel single-cell RNA-seq: an automated plate-based 3' method with FACS index sorting, early barcoding and linear amplification, developed for immune cell profiling.
items.body_md:
- Cells are FACS-sorted into 384-well plates; RT primers carry cell barcodes and UMIs; pooling, IVT amplification, 3' libraries; liquid handling robots enable thousands of cells.
- Index sorting links surface marker intensities to transcriptomes.
- Notable for immune biology (dendritic cell and macrophage subsets); MARS-seq2.0 (2019) improved cost and sensitivity.

Jaitin et al., Science 2014 (Amit lab, Weizmann Institute).

items.gloss_md: Academic droplet scRNA-seq method in which single cells are co-encapsulated with barcoded beads in nanolitre droplets, published together with inDrops in 2015 and the open-source forerunner of commercial droplet systems.
items.body_md:
- Beads carry a cell barcode (synthesised by split-and-pool) plus UMI and oligo-dT; after lysis in the droplet, mRNA hybridises to the bead; beads are pooled for RT and 3' library preparation.
- Uses home-made microfluidic devices, low reagent cost; cell capture efficiency is low (a few % of input cells) because both cells and beads are Poisson-loaded.
- Commercialised versions: Dolomite Nadia.

Macosko et al., Cell 2015 (McCarroll lab, profiled ~44,000 mouse retina cells).

attrs.anecdote: Drop-seq and inDrops appeared back-to-back in the same issue of Cell in May 2015, kick-starting high-throughput droplet single-cell genomics.

items.gloss_md: Academic droplet scRNA-seq method that uses deformable hydrogel beads with barcoded primers, published alongside Drop-seq in 2015.
items.body_md:
- Hydrogel beads pack closely and are loaded almost one per droplet (super-Poissonian), giving high cell capture efficiency; primers are released by UV.
- Barcoded RT in droplets, then CEL-seq-style IVT linear amplification and 3' libraries.
- Commercialised by 1CellBio; conceptually close to 10x Chromium gel beads.

Klein et al., Cell 2015 (Kirschner lab, Harvard).
- Like Drop-seq and 10x, it counts 3' ends with UMIs, so it suits large cell numbers rather than isoform analysis; academic setups require microfluidics expertise.

items.gloss_md: Single-cell method without physical isolation: fixed cells or nuclei are split into wells, barcoded, pooled and split again over several rounds, so each cell ends up with a unique combination of barcodes.
items.body_md:
- Round 1: barcoded RT in wells; pool; round 2/3: barcoded ligation or PCR in new wells; probability that two cells share all barcodes is small.
- Scales to millions of cells at low cost per cell; sci-RNA-seq3 profiled ~2 million cells of mouse organogenesis (Cao et al. 2019) and was used for human fetal atlases.
- Lower genes per cell than 10x; needs fixation and many cells; technical complexity in academic implementations.
- The same principle is used for chromatin (sci-ATAC-seq), methylation (sci-MET) and in commercial kits (Parse Evercode, Scale Bio).

Cao et al., Science 2017 (Shendure lab).

attrs.mnemonic: Combinatorial indexing = postal codes: country + city + street together make each address unique, even though each part alone is shared.

items.gloss_md: Split-pool ligation-based single-cell RNA-seq of fixed cells or nuclei in plates, commercialised as Parse Biosciences Evercode kits that profile up to millions of cells from many samples without special instruments.
items.body_md:
- Fixed, permeabilised cells act as their own compartments; four rounds of barcoding (RT in wells with sample-specific barcodes, then two ligation rounds, then library PCR index).
- Evercode WT kits: up to 96+ samples and from tens of thousands to millions of cells (WT Mega/Penta), only standard lab equipment; the first barcoding round encodes the sample, so multiplexing is built in.
- Fixation allows sample collection over time (clinical cohorts) and pausing.
- Lower sensitivity per cell than 10x in some comparisons; longer hands-on protocol; also TCR and CRISPR-guide versions.

Rosenberg et al., Science 2018 (Seelig lab, University of Washington).

items.gloss_md: Microwell-based single-cell platform from BD Biosciences in which cells settle into ~200,000 wells and are captured with barcoded beads, offering whole-transcriptome or targeted mRNA panels plus antibody-oligo (AbSeq) protein measurement.
items.body_md:
- Cells are loaded by gravity into a cartridge of microwells (Poisson, low multiplets), beads added, cells lysed, beads retrieved for RT.
- Targeted panels (~400–500 genes, e.g. immune response) give high sensitivity at low sequencing cost; WTA (whole transcriptome analysis) also available.
- AbSeq antibodies (oligo-tagged, like CITE-seq), Sample Tags for multiplexing, TCR/BCR assays.
- Gentle loading suits fragile cells; images of the cartridge allow cell-loading QC.

items.gloss_md: Low-cost portable microwell scRNA-seq method: cells and barcoded beads are loaded into a PDMS array of ~86,000 wells sealed with a semipermeable membrane.
items.body_md:
- Beads as in Drop-seq; the membrane seal keeps RNA in each well during lysis; arrays are simple and portable, useful for clinical samples in resource-limited settings.
- Seq-Well S3 (second-strand synthesis, 2020) improved sensitivity, e.g. for profiling skin inflammation and COVID-19 airway samples.

Gierahn et al., Nature Methods 2017 (Love and Shalek labs, MIT).
- Throughput is in the thousands to tens of thousands of cells per array, comparable to droplet methods, without expensive instruments.

items.gloss_md: scRNA-seq performed on isolated nuclei instead of whole cells, which works on frozen tissue and on cell types that do not survive dissociation.
items.body_md:
- Nuclei are released by detergent/mechanical lysis (often from snap-frozen biobank tissue) and loaded like cells (10x Chromium, Multiome, Parse).
- Advantages: works with archived frozen samples, no enzymatic dissociation stress, captures hard-to-dissociate or large cells (hepatocytes, neurons, cardiomyocytes, adipocytes, pancreatic acinar and tumour cells in fibrotic PDAC), enables Multiome (ATAC + RNA).
- Differences: nuclear RNA is rich in unspliced pre-mRNA, so intronic reads must be counted (Cell Ranger default since v7); fewer UMIs per nucleus; cytoplasmic transcripts (and mitochondrial RNA) under-represented; ambient RNA can be high.
- Cell-type proportions differ from scRNA-seq (immune cells relatively less captured than in dissociated scRNA-seq).

Especially popular in liver research (hepatocyte zonation, MASH and cirrhosis atlases) and in human brain studies.

attrs.mnemonic: Can't get the cell out alive? Take its 'brain' (the nucleus) – it still knows what the cell was transcribing.

items.gloss_md: 10x Genomics' probe-based single-cell assay for fixed cells and nuclei (including dissociated FFPE tissue), in which paired gene-specific probes hybridise, ligate and are barcoded in GEMs.
items.body_md:
- ~18,000 human (or mouse) genes targeted by pairs of probes; ligation requires both halves to bind adjacent, so fragmented RNA is fine.
- Samples are formaldehyde-fixed (stable for days to months), allowing collection over time and from multiple sites; FFPE curls can be dissociated into cells/nuclei.
- Probe barcodes allow multiplexing of many samples per channel (e.g. 4 or 16-plex) and very high cell numbers per run; high sensitivity and low ambient/dissociation artefacts.
- Limitations: only predefined genes (no unannotated transcripts, isoforms, or non-human pathogens), no V(D)J.
- Launched in 2022 (originally "Chromium Fixed RNA Profiling").

items.gloss_md: Simultaneous measurement of surface proteins and transcriptome in single cells, using antibodies conjugated to DNA barcodes (antibody-derived tags) that are captured and sequenced along with mRNA.
items.body_md:
- CITE-seq = cellular indexing of transcriptomes and epitopes by sequencing (Stoeckius et al., Nature Methods 2017); REAP-seq (Peterson et al. 2017) is a parallel method.
- Antibody oligos carry a poly(A) or capture sequence and are read as antibody-derived tags (ADTs); commercial reagents: BioLegend TotalSeq-A/-B/-C (for 10x 3' v2/v3 or 5'), BD AbSeq; panels with 100+ antibodies.
- Benefits: protein-level markers resolve immune subsets poorly separable by mRNA (CD4 vs CD8, CD45RA/RO, activation markers), and link to flow-cytometry nomenclature.
- Needs isotype controls and background correction (DSB normalisation), titrated antibodies; weighted nearest-neighbour (WNN) analysis in Seurat combines RNA and protein.

attrs.mnemonic: CITE-seq lets you 'cite' the protein name tag on the cell surface next to its transcriptome.

items.label_md: 10x Chromium Single Cell Multiome ATAC + Gene Expression
items.gloss_md: 10x Genomics assay that measures chromatin accessibility (ATAC) and the transcriptome in the same single nucleus.
items.body_md:
