- Nuclei are tagmented in bulk by Tn5 (inserting adapters into open chromatin), then partitioned into GEMs where the gel bead carries barcodes for both the ATAC fragments and poly(A) RNA.
- Gives two linked libraries per nucleus: scATAC peaks and snRNA-seq counts; analysis with Cell Ranger ARC, Signac/Seurat, ArchR, muon/MultiVI.
- Uses: link enhancers/peaks to target genes, infer gene regulatory networks (SCENIC+), identify transcription factors driving states (e.g. hepatic stellate cell activation, PDAC classical vs basal-like programmes).
- Nuclei-only; sensitivity per modality somewhat lower than single-modality assays. Launched in 2020.

items.gloss_md: ATAC-seq at single-cell resolution, measuring which genomic regions are open (accessible chromatin) in each individual cell.
items.body_md:
- Implementations: 10x Chromium Single Cell ATAC (droplets, nuclei), combinatorial indexing (sci-ATAC-seq), plate-based; the first methods were published in 2015 (Buenrostro et al.; Cusanovich et al.).
- Data are extremely sparse (each locus has only 0, 1 or 2 copies per cell); analysis uses peak or tile matrices, latent semantic indexing (TF-IDF + SVD), motif deviation scores (chromVAR), gene activity scores; tools ArchR, Signac, SnapATAC2.
- Reveals cell-type-specific enhancers and transcription factor activity; useful to map disease-risk variants (GWAS) to cell types.
- QC metrics: fragments per cell, TSS enrichment, fraction of reads in peaks, nucleosome signal.

items.gloss_md: Sequencing of rearranged T-cell receptor and B-cell receptor/antibody genes to determine clonotypes, clonal expansion and diversity, in bulk or with paired chains at single-cell level.
items.body_md:
- Targets the hypervariable CDR3 created by V(D)J recombination; a clonotype is defined by its CDR3 (and V/J genes) of both chains (TCR α/β, BCR heavy/light).
- Bulk: multiplex PCR or 5' RACE of TCRβ (e.g. Adaptive immunoSEQ) gives repertoire diversity and clone frequencies but not chain pairing.
- Single cell: 10x 5' V(D)J (paired chains + transcriptome), Smart-seq2 with TraCeR/BraCeR, BD Rhapsody and Parse TCR kits.
- Applications: tumour-infiltrating and tumour-reactive T cells, response to checkpoint inhibitors, tracking donor-reactive clones in transplant rejection and tolerance, B-cell somatic hypermutation and class switching, lymphoma clonality (MRD).
- Analysis: Immcantation, scRepertoire, MiXCR, TRUST4; antigen specificity databases (VDJdb).

attrs.mnemonic: CDR3 is the 'fingerprint' of a T- or B-cell clone: same CDR3, same family.

items.gloss_md: Labelling cells from different samples with distinct oligo-barcoded antibodies or lipids before pooling them into one single-cell run, so cells can be assigned back to samples and cross-sample doublets detected.
items.body_md:
- Antibody hashtags (HTOs, hashtag oligos) target ubiquitous surface proteins (e.g. CD298 and β2-microglobulin; BioLegend TotalSeq hashtags) (Stoeckius et al., Genome Biology 2018).
- Lipid- or cholesterol-modified oligos label any membrane, including nuclei (MULTI-seq, McGinnis et al. 2019); 10x CellPlex (CMOs) and Flex probe barcodes are commercial counterparts.
- Benefits: lower cost per sample, removal of batch effects between samples run together, "super-loading" of channels because doublets between samples are identifiable.
- Demultiplexing: HTODemux, MULTIseqDemux, hashedDrops; failures arise from poor staining or ambient tags.
- Alternative without labels: genetic demultiplexing of different donors.

items.gloss_md: Assigning cells from a pool of genetically different individuals to their donor using naturally occurring SNPs in the RNA reads, and identifying inter-individual doublets.
items.body_md:
- demuxlet (Kang et al., Nature Biotechnology 2018) uses known donor genotypes; souporcell, vireo and freemuxlet cluster cells by genotype without prior genotyping.
- Allows pooling of many patients' cells in one channel (e.g. blood from several donors), reducing cost and batch effects.
- In transplantation research it can distinguish donor- from recipient-derived cells in an allograft biopsy (and chimerism after stem cell transplantation).
- Requires enough reads covering SNPs; does not work for samples from the same individual (use hashing then).

items.gloss_md: Pooled CRISPR (or CRISPRi/a) screens in which each cell's guide RNA and its full transcriptome are read out by scRNA-seq, linking genetic perturbations to detailed expression phenotypes.
items.body_md:
- Cells are transduced at low MOI with a guide library; scRNA-seq captures both the transcriptome and the guide identity (via guide barcodes, direct capture sequences, or CROP-seq vectors).
- Readout is a full expression profile per perturbation instead of a single fitness value; enables mapping of gene functions and regulatory networks, combinatorial perturbations.
- Introduced in 2016 (Dixit et al.; Adamson et al., both Cell); genome-scale Perturb-seq (Replogle et al., Cell 2022) perturbed ~10,000 genes.
- Variants: CROP-seq, ECCITE-seq (with proteins), in vivo Perturb-seq, optical pooled screens.

items.gloss_md: A Perturb-seq-style method whose lentiviral vector places the sgRNA cassette inside a polyadenylated transcript, so the guide sequence itself is captured by standard 3' scRNA-seq.
items.body_md:
- CROP-seq = CRISPR droplet sequencing (Datlinger et al., Nature Methods 2017, Bock lab, Vienna).
- The guide is copied into the 3' LTR during lentiviral integration: one copy is transcribed by the U6 promoter as functional sgRNA, the other appears in a Pol II poly(A) transcript.
- Advantage: no separate guide barcode (no barcode–guide swapping by lentiviral recombination); compatible with any poly(A)-capture scRNA-seq.

items.gloss_md: Measuring more than one molecular layer (RNA, chromatin, protein, DNA, methylation, receptor sequences, perturbations, spatial position) in the same individual cell.
items.body_md:
- RNA + protein: CITE-seq/REAP-seq, BD AbSeq, Mission Bio Tapestri (DNA + protein).
- RNA + chromatin: 10x Multiome (ATAC + GEX), SHARE-seq, SNARE-seq; RNA + histone marks: single-cell CUT&Tag combinations.
- RNA + DNA/methylation: G&T-seq (genome and transcriptome), scNMT-seq (nucleosome, methylation, transcription).
- RNA + receptors/guides: 10x 5' V(D)J, Perturb-seq.
- Analysis: weighted nearest neighbours (Seurat WNN), MOFA+, totalVI/MultiVI; also "diagonal" integration of different modalities measured in different cells.
- Nature Methods named single-cell multimodal omics the Method of the Year 2019.

attrs.anecdote: Nature Methods chose single-cell multimodal omics as Method of the Year 2019, one year before spatially resolved transcriptomics (2020).

items.gloss_md: Sequencing of the genome (or targeted regions) of individual cells to detect copy-number changes and mutations per cell, revealing clonal architecture and evolution.
items.body_md:
- Whole-genome amplification needed (MDA, MALBAC, PTA, or direct tagmentation such as DLP+), with uneven coverage and allelic dropout as main artefacts.
- Low-pass single-cell WGS calls copy-number profiles of thousands of cells; targeted amplicon methods (Mission Bio Tapestri) genotype hundreds of loci plus surface proteins in thousands of cells – used in AML and clonal haematopoiesis.
- Copy-number can also be inferred from scRNA-seq (inferCNV, CopyKAT) to separate malignant from normal cells, e.g. in PDAC.
- Applications: tumour heterogeneity, clonal evolution, somatic mosaicism in normal tissues.

items.gloss_md: Bisulfite- or enzyme-based sequencing of DNA methylation in individual cells (e.g. scBS-seq, scRRBS, snmC-seq, sci-MET), used to define epigenetic cell identities and lineages.
items.body_md:
- Each cell yields sparse CpG coverage (typically a few to ~20 % of CpGs); analysis aggregates over regions or cells.
- Methods: scBS-seq (Smallwood et al. 2014), scRRBS, snmC-seq (neurons), sci-MET (combinatorial indexing); multi-omic scNMT-seq (methylation + accessibility + RNA).
- Uses: developmental biology, neuronal subtypes, epigenetic heterogeneity in cancer, lineage tracing by stochastic epimutations.
- Methylation patterns are stable cell-identity marks, so they can classify cell types even with sparse data, but the bisulfite step destroys much of the DNA of a single cell.

items.gloss_md: Methods that measure gene expression while keeping the position of the RNA in an intact tissue section, linking transcriptomes to histology and cell neighbourhoods.
items.body_md:
Three main families:
- Sequencing-based capture: RNA from the section is captured on arrays of spatially barcoded spots or beads and sequenced (10x Visium/Visium HD, Slide-seq, Stereo-seq). Whole transcriptome, resolution from 55 µm spots to subcellular bins.
- Imaging-based in situ: transcripts are detected directly in the tissue by repeated rounds of fluorescent hybridisation or in situ sequencing (MERFISH/MERSCOPE, seqFISH, 10x Xenium, CosMx SMI). Single-cell/subcellular resolution, panels of hundreds to a few thousand genes (now approaching whole transcriptome).
- Region-of-interest profiling: selected areas are profiled with barcoded probes (GeoMx DSP) or by laser capture microdissection.
- Analysis: spot deconvolution (cell2location, RCTD), cell segmentation, spatially variable genes, niches/neighbourhoods, cell–cell interactions, integration with scRNA-seq references.
- Trade-offs: genes measured vs resolution vs area vs cost; FFPE compatibility varies.

Nature Methods' Method of the Year 2020. The term "Spatial Transcriptomics" originally referred to the method of Ståhl et al. (Science 2016, Lundeberg lab), the precursor of Visium.

attrs.mnemonic: Three families, three verbs: capture (Visium), image (Xenium, MERFISH, CosMx), select (GeoMx).
attrs.anecdote: Spatially resolved transcriptomics was Nature Methods' Method of the Year 2020; the 2016 Spatial Transcriptomics technology came from Joakim Lundeberg's group at KTH Stockholm, and the spin-off company was bought by 10x Genomics in 2018 to make Visium.

items.gloss_md: Sequencing-based spatial transcriptomics on glass slides carrying ~5,000 barcoded 55-µm spots per capture area; the tissue's RNA (or probes) is captured by the spots, sequenced and mapped back onto the H&E image.
items.body_md:
- Standard Visium (v1, 2019): 6.5 × 6.5 mm capture areas, spots 55 µm in diameter, 100 µm centre-to-centre; each spot contains about 1–10 cells, so results are mixtures that need deconvolution with scRNA-seq references (cell2location, RCTD, SPOTlight).
- Chemistry: originally poly(dT) capture on fresh-frozen tissue; Visium for FFPE (2021) uses whole-transcriptome probe pairs (~18,000 genes), now the main mode.
- Workflow: section on slide → H&E or IF imaging → permeabilisation/probe release → barcoded capture → library → sequencing → Space Ranger → analysis in Seurat/Squidpy/Loupe Browser.
- Strengths: unbiased whole transcriptome, standard histology on the same section, broad adoption.
- Limitations: not single-cell (v1), gaps between spots, limited area, tissue quality requirements; succeeded by CytAssist-based v2 and Visium HD.

Used e.g. to map PDAC tumour–stroma niches, liver zonation and fibrotic scars.

attrs.mnemonic: Visium v1 numbers: 55 µm spots, 100 µm apart, ~5,000 spots – 'fifty-five, hundred, five thousand'.

items.gloss_md: A 10x Genomics instrument that transfers gene-expression probes from a tissue section on a standard glass slide onto a Visium capture slide, enabling use of archived slides and larger capture areas.
items.body_md:
- Sections can be cut onto ordinary microscope slides (also older archival sections), stained/imaged first, then probes are released and transferred to the Visium slide in the CytAssist.
- Enables Visium v2 slides with 6.5 × 6.5 mm or 11 × 11 mm capture areas (~14,000 spots), higher sensitivity, FFPE, fixed-frozen and fresh-frozen samples, and protein co-detection (oligo-tagged antibody panels).
- Required for Visium HD.
- Launched in 2022.

items.gloss_md: High-definition version of 10x Visium with a continuous lawn of 2 × 2 µm barcoded squares, giving whole-transcriptome spatial data at single-cell scale.
items.body_md:
- ~11 million 2-µm squares per 6.5 × 6.5 mm capture area, without gaps; data are usually analysed in 8 × 8 µm bins (or 16 µm) or aggregated into segmented cells (nuclei segmentation from H&E/IF).
- Probe-based whole transcriptome (~18,000 genes) for FFPE, fixed-frozen and fresh-frozen tissue via CytAssist; a 3' poly(A)-capture version was added later.
- Bridges the gap between spot-based Visium (55 µm) and imaging platforms (subcellular but targeted panels).
- Challenges: per-bin sparsity, lateral diffusion of transcripts, segmentation and assignment to cells, large data volumes.
- Launched in 2024.

attrs.mnemonic: HD = 2 µm squares, analysed as 8 µm bins: 'two to see, eight to analyse'.

items.gloss_md: Imaging-based spatial platform that detects hundreds to thousands of target RNAs directly in tissue at subcellular resolution using padlock probes, rolling-circle amplification and cyclic fluorescent decoding.
items.body_md:
- Padlock probes bind target RNA and are ligated into circles, amplified in situ by rolling-circle amplification; gene-specific barcodes are read over many cycles of fluorescent probe hybridisation and imaging in the Xenium Analyzer.
- Panels: pre-designed tissue panels (~250–480 genes) plus custom add-ons; Xenium Prime 5K (~5,000 genes, 2024); FFPE and fresh-frozen.
- Cell segmentation using nuclear (DAPI) and multimodal membrane/cytoplasm stains; output transcripts with x/y/z coordinates and cell-feature matrices.
- The section remains intact after the run, so H&E or IF can be done on the same slide.
- Strengths: true single-cell and subcellular resolution, large areas, high sensitivity; limitations: targeted genes only, segmentation errors, run time and cost.
- Commercially available since 2022/2023; 10x acquired the in-situ sequencing company CARTANA (2020) for the underlying chemistry.

items.gloss_md: NanoString/Bruker spatial platform in which a tissue section is stained with fluorescent morphology markers, the user selects regions of interest, and UV light releases photocleavable oligo barcodes from RNA probes or antibodies in each region for counting.
items.body_md:
- Morphology markers (e.g. PanCK for epithelium/tumour, CD45 for immune cells, SMA for fibroblasts, DNA stain) guide selection of regions of interest (ROIs) and segmentation into areas of illumination (AOIs) such as tumour vs stroma compartments.
- Probes carry UV-photocleavable barcodes; a microcapillary aspirates released barcodes per AOI, which are counted by NGS (or nCounter).
- Content: Whole Transcriptome Atlas (~18,000 human genes), targeted RNA panels, ~50–150 protein targets; FFPE compatible.
- Resolution is region-level (typically 50–600 µm ROIs, tens to hundreds of cells), not single cell; very good for compartment-specific comparisons in clinical cohorts and TMAs.
- Analysis: Q3 normalisation, GeomxTools, standR, spatial deconvolution (SpatialDecon).

attrs.mnemonic: GeoMx = you are the geographer: you draw the borders (ROIs) and it counts what lives inside.

items.gloss_md: NanoString/Bruker imaging-based in situ platform that measures up to thousands of RNAs (and ~60–100 proteins) at single-cell and subcellular resolution in FFPE tissue by cyclic hybridisation of fluorescent reporters.
items.body_md:
- Gene-specific ISH probes carry readout domains; many cycles of fluorescent reporter hybridisation and imaging decode each transcript's identity (a colour/position code).
- RNA panels: ~1,000-plex Universal Cell Characterization, 6K Discovery panel, and later a whole-transcriptome panel; protein panels of ~60+ antibodies.
- Cell segmentation with membrane and nuclear stains; analysis in AtoMx Spatial Informatics Platform.
- Strengths: high plex for imaging, FFPE, TMAs; limitations: field-of-view based (selected areas), long run times, segmentation and background (negative probe) handling.
- Introduced in 2021–2022 (He et al., Nature Biotechnology 2022).

items.gloss_md: Multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridisation: each RNA species gets a binary barcode read out over sequential rounds of hybridisation and imaging, with error-correcting codes, allowing hundreds to thousands of genes to be imaged with single-molecule resolution.
items.body_md:
- Encoding probes tile each target RNA; readout probes for one bit at a time are hybridised, imaged and bleached/removed; the on/off pattern over rounds forms the barcode; code words separated by Hamming distance 4 allow error detection/correction.
- Single-molecule sensitivity close to smFISH, subcellular localisation, large tissue areas.
- Commercialised by Vizgen as MERSCOPE (2021): panels of ~140–1,000 genes, FFPE and fresh-frozen, protein co-staining, cell boundary stains.
- Limitations: targeted panel design, optical crowding of highly expressed genes, segmentation.

Chen, Boettiger, Moffitt, Wang & Zhuang, Science 2015 (Xiaowei Zhuang lab, Harvard).

attrs.mnemonic: MERFISH reads RNA in Morse code: on–off flashes over rounds spell each gene's barcode.

items.gloss_md: Sequential FISH, an imaging method in which RNA identity is encoded by the sequence of colours over successive hybridisation rounds, scaling to thousands of genes in single cells in situ.
items.body_md:
- Colour barcodes (e.g. F colours over N rounds give F^N codes); seqFISH+ (Eng et al., Nature 2019) used "pseudocolours" across many channels to image 10,000 genes in single cells.
- Also applied to chromatin tracing (DNA seqFISH+) and intron (nascent transcription) imaging.
- Developed by Long Cai's lab (Caltech) from 2014 (Lubeck et al., Nature Methods); commercial by Spatial Genomics.

items.gloss_md: Sequencing-based spatial transcriptomics using a 'puck' of randomly deposited 10-µm DNA-barcoded beads whose positions are determined by in situ sequencing before tissue RNA is transferred onto them.
items.body_md:
- ~10 µm resolution (near single-cell), unbiased 3' whole transcriptome; beads are decoded optically, then a fresh-frozen section is melted onto the puck and RNA captured.
- Slide-seqV2 (Stickels et al., Nature Biotechnology 2021) improved RNA capture about tenfold over Slide-seq (Rodriques et al., Science 2019, Chen and Macosko labs, Broad Institute).
- Commercialised as Curio Seeker; sparse counts per bead; extensions Slide-tags (nuclei tagged with spatial barcodes for snRNA-seq).

items.gloss_md: BGI/MGI's spatial transcriptomics method that captures tissue RNA on DNA-nanoball arrays with sub-micrometre spot spacing over areas up to centimetres, giving whole-transcriptome data at subcellular scale.
items.body_md:
- SpaTial Enhanced Resolution Omics-sequencing (Chen et al., Cell 2022): DNA nanoballs with coordinate barcodes on patterned chips (spots ~0.2 µm, 0.5 µm centre-to-centre); poly(dT) capture.
- Data analysed in bins (e.g. bin50 = 50 × 50 DNBs ≈ 25 µm) or segmented cells; very large chips allow whole mouse embryos or large human sections.
- Commercial name STOmics; FFPE and multi-omic extensions exist.
- Practical issues: data size, sparse per-spot counts, availability outside China-linked supply chains.

items.gloss_md: Highly multiplexed tissue imaging in which antibodies tagged with DNA barcodes are applied at once and revealed cycle by cycle with complementary fluorescent reporters, imaging 40–100+ proteins on one section.
items.body_md:
- CODEX = co-detection by indexing (Goltsev et al., Cell 2018, Nolan lab, Stanford); commercialised by Akoya Biosciences as PhenoCycler and PhenoCycler-Fusion (whole-slide).
- Single-cell resolution spatial proteomics on FFPE or frozen tissue; cell phenotyping and neighbourhood analysis (e.g. "cellular neighbourhoods" in colorectal cancer, Schürch et al. 2020).
- Analysis: segmentation (Mesmer/DeepCell), clustering of marker intensities, spatial statistics.
- Compared with IMC/MIBI: fluorescence-based, faster, larger areas; autofluorescence and antibody validation are the main issues.

items.gloss_md: Tissue imaging in which sections stained with metal-isotope-tagged antibodies are ablated by a laser spot by spot and the metals are measured by time-of-flight mass cytometry, giving ~40 protein markers at 1-µm resolution.
items.body_md:
- Lanthanide-labelled antibodies (as in CyTOF), laser ablation of 1-µm pixels, CyTOF detection; almost no spectral overlap and no autofluorescence.
- Standard BioTools (formerly Fluidigm) Hyperion / Hyperion XTi Imaging System; FFPE and frozen tissue.
- Slow (areas of mm² take hours) and destructive, so usually regions or TMA cores; analysis pipelines steinbock, imcRtools, histoCAT.
- Used for tumour immune microenvironment atlases (e.g. breast cancer, Jackson et al. 2020) and inflammatory tissues.

Giesen et al., Nature Methods 2014 (Bodenmiller lab, Zurich).

attrs.mnemonic: IMC = CyTOF with a laser eraser: it rubs the tissue away pixel by pixel and weighs the metals.

items.gloss_md: Tissue imaging that uses a primary ion beam to release metal-tagged antibody labels from the section, measured by time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry for ~40 proteins at subcellular resolution.
items.body_md:
- Similar reagents to IMC (lanthanide-conjugated antibodies) but secondary ion mass spectrometry with higher resolution (down to ~300 nm) and faster acquisition.
- Commercialised by Ionpath (MIBIscope).
- Classic study: Keren et al., Cell 2018 – immune architecture of triple-negative breast cancer (compartmentalised vs mixed tumours).

Angelo et al., Nature Medicine 2014 (Bendall lab, Stanford).
- Like IMC it avoids autofluorescence and spectral overlap, is destructive, and covers only selected fields of view per run; image analysis requires cell segmentation and phenotyping pipelines.

items.gloss_md: Staining one tissue section for several proteins (typically 6–9) with fluorescent labels, most commonly by sequential tyramide signal amplification (Opal), and imaging with multispectral unmixing.
items.body_md:
- Opal workflow (Akoya): primary antibody → HRP secondary → fluorophore-tyramide deposits covalently near the epitope → heat stripping of antibodies → next marker; antibodies from the same species can be reused.
- Imaging on multispectral scanners (Vectra Polaris / PhenoImager HT), spectral unmixing and autofluorescence removal; analysis in inForm, HALO, QuPath.
- Typical panels: CD8, CD4, FoxP3, CD68, PD-L1, PanCK + DAPI for immune contexture and checkpoint biomarker research; spatial metrics such as distances of CD8 T cells to tumour cells.
- Other approaches: cyclic IF (CyCIF, t-CyCIF), CODEX/PhenoCycler, Lunaphore COMET (sequential IF on a chip), MACSima.

items.gloss_md: Detection of a specific protein in tissue sections with a labelled antibody, visualised by an enzyme-generated coloured precipitate (usually brown DAB) under the light microscope – the routine protein assay of pathology.
items.body_md:
- Workflow on FFPE sections: deparaffinisation → heat-induced epitope retrieval → primary antibody → polymer/HRP detection system → DAB chromogen (brown) → haematoxylin counterstain (blue nuclei); automated stainers (Roche Ventana, Leica BOND, Agilent Dako).
- Read-out is semi-quantitative: percentage of positive cells, intensity, localisation (nuclear/cytoplasmic/membranous); scores such as H-score, Allred, PD-L1 TPS and CPS; Ki-67 index.
- Clinical examples: tumour typing (cytokeratins CK7/CK19/CK20, CDX2), PDAC loss of SMAD4 (DPC4) and aberrant p53, mismatch-repair proteins (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2 – dMMR/MSI screening), PD-L1 (22C3) for checkpoint therapy, HER2; in transplant biopsies C4d (peritubular capillaries) as a marker of antibody-mediated rejection; in liver CK7 for ductular reaction, glutamine synthetase and glypican-3 for hepatocellular lesions.
- Limitations: antibody specificity and validation, pre-analytic fixation effects, observer variability; digital image analysis helps.

attrs.mnemonic: IHC = brown means yes: DAB-brown is positive, haematoxylin-blue is the background nuclei.
attrs.anecdote: Albert Coons labelled antibodies with fluorescein in 1941 to detect pneumococcal antigen in tissue – the birth of immunofluorescence; the enzyme (peroxidase) label that pathologists use today followed in the 1960s (Nakane and Pierce, 1966).

items.gloss_md: Detection of specific DNA or RNA sequences directly in cells or tissue sections with labelled complementary nucleic acid probes, visualised by chromogen (CISH) or fluorescence (FISH).
items.body_md:
- RNA ISH shows where a gene is expressed (e.g. which cells transcribe a cytokine), useful when no good antibody exists or for secreted proteins.
- DNA ISH shows gene copy number and rearrangements in interphase nuclei (FISH for HER2 amplification, ALK/ROS1 break-apart).
- Clinically important: EBER ISH (Epstein–Barr virus-encoded small RNAs) to diagnose EBV-associated post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD); kappa/lambda light-chain ISH for clonality; HPV ISH.
- Modern sensitive variants: RNAscope, BaseScope, smFISH; high-plex imaging spatial methods (MERFISH, Xenium, CosMx) are its multiplexed descendants.

First described in 1969 (Gall & Pardue; John et al.) with radioactive probes.

items.gloss_md: In situ hybridisation with fluorescently labelled DNA probes to visualise chromosomal regions, gene copy number and rearrangements in single nuclei.
items.body_md:
- Probe types: locus-specific, centromeric (CEP), whole-chromosome paints; break-apart probes (split signals = rearrangement, e.g. ALK, ROS1, BCL2, MYC) and dual-fusion probes (e.g. BCR::ABL1).
- Works on interphase nuclei in FFPE sections, cytology, blood and marrow smears – no dividing cells needed, unlike karyotyping.
- Clinical uses: HER2 (ERBB2) amplification (HER2/CEP17 ratio), lymphoma and leukaemia translocations, sex-chromosome chimerism after sex-mismatched transplantation, prenatal aneuploidy screening, UroVysion bladder cancer test.
- Resolution: detects specific known targets only; a genome-wide alternative is array CGH or sequencing.

attrs.mnemonic: Break-apart probe: red and green normally together (yellow); if they 'break apart', the gene is rearranged.

items.gloss_md: A commercial RNA in situ hybridisation method (ACD, Bio-Techne) whose 'double-Z' probe design and branched signal amplification detect single RNA molecules as dots in FFPE tissue with high specificity.
items.body_md:
- Pairs of Z-shaped probes must bind adjacent on the target before the pre-amplifier can bind (like a two-key lock), suppressing background; amplifiers and labelled probes create a dot per molecule.
- Chromogenic (brown/red, duplex) and fluorescent (multiplex up to 4, HiPlex up to 12+) versions; automated on Leica BOND and Roche Ventana.
- BaseScope detects short targets such as splice junctions, point mutations or fusion junctions; miRNAscope for small RNAs.
- Uses: validate scRNA-seq markers in tissue, localise cytokine/chemokine expression, viral RNA (HPV, SARS-CoV-2), targets without good antibodies.

Wang et al., Journal of Molecular Diagnostics 2012.

attrs.mnemonic: Double-Z = two keys for one lock: signal only when both halves bind side by side.

items.gloss_md: Imaging of individual mRNA molecules in fixed cells using dozens of short fluorescently labelled oligonucleotide probes tiling one transcript, so each molecule appears as a diffraction-limited dot.
items.body_md:
- ~30–50 probes of ~20 nt per mRNA (Raj et al., Nature Methods 2008, building on Femino et al. 1998); dots are counted per cell, giving absolute transcript numbers.
- Gold standard for transcript counting and subcellular localisation; used to study transcriptional bursting and cell-to-cell variability, and to validate single-cell sequencing.
- Low plex (a few genes per round) – the starting point for MERFISH, seqFISH and other multiplexed imaging methods.
- Commercial probes: Stellaris (Biosearch).

items.gloss_md: The standard histological stain, in which haematoxylin colours nuclei blue-purple and eosin colours cytoplasm and extracellular matrix pink, forming the basis of almost all histopathological diagnosis.
items.body_md:
- Haematoxylin (with a mordant) binds basophilic structures such as chromatin; eosin binds acidophilic/eosinophilic proteins in cytoplasm, collagen, red blood cells.
- Pathologists judge architecture, cell morphology, inflammation, necrosis, fibrosis and tumour grade on H&E; in liver: steatosis, ballooning, lobular inflammation (NAS scoring of MASLD), in transplant biopsies: tubulitis and interstitial inflammation (Banff).
- Special stains supplement H&E: Masson's trichrome and Sirius red (collagen/fibrosis staging), reticulin, Perls' Prussian blue (iron), PAS/PAS-D (glycogen, α1-antitrypsin globules), orcein/rhodanine (copper).
- H&E images are the reference layer in spatial transcriptomics (Visium) and the input of computational pathology/deep learning.

attrs.mnemonic: Haematoxylin = 'H' for 'Heads' (nuclei, blue); Eosin = 'E' for 'Everything else' (pink).
attrs.anecdote: Haematoxylin is extracted from the heartwood of the logwood tree (Haematoxylum campechianum), which was originally prized as a textile dye; the H&E combination has been in routine use since the late 19th century.

items.gloss_md: The standard way pathology preserves tissue: fixation in formalin (crosslinking proteins and nucleic acids) followed by embedding in paraffin wax, giving blocks that keep morphology for decades at room temperature.
items.body_md:
- Formaldehyde forms methylene bridges between proteins and nucleic acids; RNA and DNA become fragmented and chemically modified (C>T deamination artefacts in sequencing).
- Archives of millions of FFPE blocks with clinical follow-up make FFPE the key material for translational studies (e.g. resected PDAC, liver biopsies, transplant biopsies).
- Molecular methods that work well on FFPE: IHC, ISH/FISH, targeted DNA panels, capture or probe-based RNA methods (exome-capture RNA-seq, NanoString, 10x Flex, Visium FFPE, GeoMx, Xenium, CosMx), RNA quality checked by DV200.
- Alternative: fresh-frozen (snap-frozen, OCT-embedded cryosections) – better nucleic acids, worse morphology, needs −80 °C storage.
- Pre-analytics matter: cold ischaemia time, fixation duration (ideally 6–72 h in 10 % neutral buffered formalin), block age.

attrs.mnemonic: FFPE = 'Forever Fixed, Poorly Extractable': morphology lasts forever, nucleic acids come out in pieces.

items.gloss_md: Scanning of entire glass slides at high resolution into gigapixel digital images for viewing, image analysis and AI in pathology.
items.body_md:
- Scanners (e.g. Leica Aperio, Hamamatsu NanoZoomer, Roche Ventana DP, 3DHISTECH) capture brightfield (H&E, IHC) or fluorescence slides at 20× or 40× (~0.5 or ~0.25 µm/pixel).
- Formats: vendor pyramidal files (SVS, NDPI, MRXS) and OME-TIFF; open-source viewers/analysis: QuPath, OpenSlide.
- Uses: digital sign-out and teleconsultation, quantitative IHC (Ki-67, PD-L1), tumour-cellularity estimation before sequencing, deep-learning prediction of molecular features (e.g. MSI from H&E), registration with spatial omics.

items.gloss_md: A paraffin block assembled from small cylindrical cores (typically 0.6–2 mm) of dozens to hundreds of different tumour or tissue blocks, so that all can be stained and analysed on one slide.
items.body_md:
- Enables high-throughput IHC, ISH and spatial omics (GeoMx, CosMx, IMC) across large clinical cohorts with identical staining conditions.
- Limitation: a core samples only a small part of a heterogeneous tumour; usually 2–4 cores per case are taken.
- Introduced by Kononen et al., Nature Medicine 1998 (Kallioniemi lab).
- Construction uses manual or automated arrayers that punch donor cores from marked tumour areas on the H&E slide.
- Typical use: correlating a marker's IHC score with survival in hundreds of resected tumours (e.g. PDAC or HCC cohorts).

items.gloss_md: Microscope-guided isolation of specific cells or regions from tissue sections with a laser, so that e.g. tumour epithelium and stroma can be analysed separately.
items.body_md:
- Systems: Leica LMD (cutting and gravity), Zeiss PALM (laser pressure catapulting), Arcturus (thermoplastic film capture).
- Downstream: DNA/RNA sequencing, proteomics, methylation of pure compartments; important in PDAC, where tumour cellularity is often low and stroma dominates bulk profiles (e.g. Moffitt et al. 2015 virtual microdissection is the computational counterpart).
- Low input requires sensitive library preparation; time-consuming; the computational alternative is deconvolution.
- Spatially resolved "LCM-seq" and Geo-seq are research variants.

items.gloss_md: Label-free spatial mapping of metabolites, lipids, drugs, glycans or peptides in tissue sections by acquiring MALDI mass spectra pixel by pixel.
items.body_md:
- A matrix is sprayed onto the section; a laser rasters across it, desorbing and ionising molecules (MALDI) whose m/z is measured (TOF, Orbitrap, FTICR, timsTOF fleX); each m/z gives an ion image.
- Lateral resolution typically 5–50 µm; untargeted, hundreds to thousands of features, but identification is hard without MS/MS.
- Uses: lipid zonation in liver, drug distribution, N-glycan imaging in FFPE, tumour margins; DESI is an ambient-ionisation alternative.
- Can be co-registered with H&E and spatial transcriptomics.

items.gloss_md: Measurement of light scatter and fluorescence of individual cells as they pass in a fluid stream through laser beams, used to count and characterise cell populations by size, granularity and fluorescent-antibody-labelled markers.
items.body_md:
- Forward scatter (FSC) ≈ cell size, side scatter (SSC) ≈ granularity/complexity; fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies against CD markers and intracellular proteins (after fixation/permeabilisation: FoxP3, Ki-67, cytokines, phospho-proteins); viability dyes exclude dead cells.
- Thousands of cells per second, millions per sample; conventional instruments measure ~10–30 colours (BD FACSCanto/LSRFortessa/FACSymphony, Beckman CytoFLEX); spectral cytometers 40+.
- Analysis: compensation, hierarchical gating (FlowJo, FCS Express) or high-dimensional clustering (FlowSOM, UMAP); data in FCS files.
- Clinical: immunophenotyping of leukaemias/lymphomas and minimal residual disease, CD4 counts (HIV), CD34 stem cell counts, paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria; in transplantation the flow cytometric crossmatch (FCXM) detects donor-specific antibodies against donor lymphocytes, and lymphocyte subset monitoring under immunosuppression.
- Limitations: needs single-cell suspensions (no tissue context), spectral overlap, panel design effort, antibody/fluorochrome availability.

attrs.mnemonic: FSC = Fat (size), SSC = Spiky (granularity): forward sees how big, side sees how grainy.
attrs.anecdote: Wallace Coulter patented counting cells by electrical impedance (the Coulter principle) in 1953; the Herzenberg lab at Stanford developed the fluorescence-activated cell sorter around 1969–1972 and coined the term 'FACS', later trademarked by Becton Dickinson.

items.gloss_md: Flow cytometry with physical sorting: droplets containing cells with a chosen fluorescence/scatter profile are electrically charged and deflected into collection tubes or plate wells.
items.body_md:
- The stream is broken into droplets by vibration; when a cell matching the sort gate is in a droplet, it is charged and deflected by electrostatic plates.
- Yields highly pure (>95 %) live populations for culture, transplantation experiments, bulk RNA-seq of defined subsets or single-cell sorting into plates (Smart-seq2, index sorting).
- Instruments: BD FACSAria, Beckman MoFlo, Sony SH800/MA900; imaging sorters (BD FACSDiscover S8).
- Alternatives: magnetic-activated cell sorting (MACS, Miltenyi) – faster, gentler, lower purity and fewer parameters.
- "FACS" is often (loosely) used for any flow cytometry, especially in German labs ("FACS-Analyse").

items.gloss_md: Flow cytometry that records each cell's full fluorescence emission spectrum across many detectors and separates fluorochromes by spectral unmixing, allowing 30–40+ colours in one tube.
items.body_md:
- Instead of one detector per fluorochrome with band-pass filters, arrays of detectors (e.g. Cytek Aurora with up to 5 lasers and 64 detectors) capture the spectral signature; reference controls (single stains, unstained) define signatures for unmixing.
- Cell autofluorescence can be extracted as its own "fluorochrome", improving resolution in autofluorescent tissues (lung, liver macrophages).
- Instruments: Cytek Aurora/Northern Lights, Sony ID7000, BD FACSymphony A5 SE, BD FACSDiscover; spectral sorters (Aurora CS).
- Enables deep immunophenotyping from small samples (e.g. biopsies, paediatric blood) with high-dimensional analysis (UMAP, FlowSOM).

items.gloss_md: The sequence of 2D plots and regions (gates) used to select a cell population step by step, e.g. cells → single cells → live cells → CD45+ → CD3+ → CD4+.
items.body_md:
- Typical start: FSC-A vs SSC-A (exclude debris), FSC-H vs FSC-A (singlets/exclude doublets), viability dye negative (live), then lineage markers.
- Controls: unstained, fluorescence-minus-one (FMO) controls to set boundaries for dim or continuous markers, isotype controls (of limited value), biological reference samples.
- Manual gating is subjective; automated gating/clustering (FlowSOM, PhenoGraph, OpenCyto) and back-gating improve reproducibility.
- Population frequencies are reported as % of parent or % of live/CD45+ cells – always check the denominator.

attrs.mnemonic: Gate like a bouncer: first 'are you a cell?', then 'are you alone?' (singlet), 'are you alive?', and only then 'which club (lineage) do you belong to?'.

items.gloss_md: Mathematical correction in conventional flow cytometry for the part of a fluorochrome's emission that is detected in other fluorochromes' channels.
items.body_md:
- Single-stained controls (cells or beads) for each fluorochrome define a spillover matrix; its inverse is applied to all events.
- Compensation corrects the means but not the spread: spillover spreading error widens negative populations and limits resolution of dim markers – panel design places bright fluorochromes on low-abundance markers and avoids strongly overlapping dyes on co-expressed markers.
- Spectral cytometers replace compensation by unmixing; mass cytometry has little spillover (some isotope impurity and oxidation, M+16).

items.gloss_md: Single-cell cytometry in which antibodies are labelled with heavy-metal isotopes instead of fluorochromes and each cell is atomised, ionised and analysed by time-of-flight mass spectrometry, measuring ~40–50 markers per cell.
items.body_md:
- Lanthanide and other metal isotopes give discrete mass channels with minimal overlap and no autofluorescence; cisplatin marks dead cells, iridium DNA intercalator identifies nucleated cells; palladium barcoding multiplexes samples.
- Throughput ~300–1,000 cells per second (slower than flow); cells are destroyed (no sorting); no scatter parameters; lower sensitivity for dim markers than the best fluorochromes.
- Instruments: Fluidigm (now Standard BioTools) CyTOF 2, Helios, CyTOF XT. Same detection principle in imaging mass cytometry (Hyperion).
- Analysis: normalisation beads, debarcoding, viSNE/UMAP, FlowSOM, CITRUS; well suited to deep immune profiling in clinical trials and transplantation/immunosuppression studies.

Bandura et al. 2009 (Tanner lab, Toronto); landmark application Bendall et al., Science 2011 (Nolan lab).

attrs.mnemonic: CyTOF = Cytometry by Time-Of-Flight: heavier metals fly slower – the arrival time tells which antibody it was.

items.gloss_md: Large-scale identification and quantification of proteins by digesting them into peptides, separating these by liquid chromatography and measuring their masses and fragment spectra by tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS).
items.body_md:
- Bottom-up ("shotgun") workflow: protein extraction → trypsin digestion (cuts after K/R) → nanoLC → electrospray ionisation → MS1 survey scan → MS/MS fragmentation → database search (MaxQuant/Andromeda, Mascot, Sequest, FragPipe/MSFragger; DIA-NN, Spectronaut) → peptide-spectrum matches at 1 % FDR (target–decoy) → protein inference and quantification.
- Acquisition: DDA, DIA (SWATH), targeted SRM/PRM. Quantification: label-free (LFQ), isobaric labels (TMT/iTRAQ), metabolic labels (SILAC).
- Depth: ~8,000–10,000 proteins in cell lines and tissues; plasma is hard because of its >10 orders of magnitude dynamic range (albumin and a few proteins dominate), requiring depletion or enrichment (e.g. nanoparticle coronas).
- Instruments: Thermo Orbitrap (Exploris, Astral), Bruker timsTOF (ion mobility), SCIEX ZenoTOF/TripleTOF; also top-down (intact proteins), PTM-omics, interactomics (AP-MS), structural MS.
- Data repositories: PRIDE (ProteomeXchange).

attrs.mnemonic: Bottom-up = 'shred the book (trypsin), read the snippets (peptides), reassemble which book it was (protein inference)'.
attrs.anecdote: John Fenn (electrospray) and Koichi Tanaka (soft laser desorption) shared the 2002 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for methods to ionise intact large biomolecules – the foundation of protein mass spectrometry; Tanaka was a company engineer without a PhD.

items.gloss_md: Two stages of mass analysis: a precursor ion is selected (MS1), fragmented, and its fragment ions measured (MS2), revealing structure – for peptides, the amino-acid sequence.
items.body_md:
- Fragmentation methods: CID and HCD (collisions with gas; peptides break at amide bonds into b- and y-ions), ETD/EThcD (preserve labile PTMs such as phosphorylation, glycosylation).
- Mass differences between consecutive b- or y-ions correspond to amino-acid residues; search engines match observed spectra to theoretical spectra from a protein database.
- Instrument types: triple quadrupole (targeted), Q-TOF, Orbitrap hybrids, ion traps, timsTOF (trapped ion mobility adds a separation dimension).
- Also the basis of targeted clinical assays (LC-MS/MS for immunosuppressant drug levels such as tacrolimus, newborn screening, steroid panels).

attrs.mnemonic: b-ions from the 'beginning' (N-terminus), y-ions from the other end (C-terminus).

items.gloss_md: MS acquisition mode in which, after each MS1 survey scan, the instrument selects the N most intense precursor ions (top-N) for fragmentation, giving clean MS2 spectra of individual peptides.
items.body_md:
- Dynamic exclusion avoids repeatedly fragmenting the same precursor.
- Strengths: simple interpretation (one precursor per spectrum), the classic workflow for discovery and building spectral libraries; combined with TMT for multiplexing.
- Weakness: stochastic precursor selection → peptides identified in some runs and not others → many missing values in label-free cohorts (partly rescued by match-between-runs).
- Typical instrument cycle: one MS1 scan followed by 10–20 MS2 scans, repeated every 1–2 seconds over a 1–2 h LC gradient.
- Analysed with MaxQuant, FragPipe or Proteome Discoverer.

attrs.mnemonic: DDA = 'pick the loudest' – it only fragments what shouts the most in MS1.

items.gloss_md: MS acquisition mode that systematically fragments all precursors within consecutive m/z windows, independent of their intensity, giving complete, reproducible MS2 data that are deconvolved computationally.
items.body_md:
- Windows (e.g. 8–25 m/z wide, or variable) cycle over the mass range each few seconds; each MS2 spectrum contains fragments of many co-isolated peptides.
- Analysis with spectral libraries (from DDA) or library-free/predicted libraries: DIA-NN, Spectronaut, OpenSWATH, EncyclopeDIA.
- Strengths: far fewer missing values, better quantitative precision, scalable to large clinical cohorts (plasma proteomics); now the default for many label-free studies, especially on Orbitrap Astral and timsTOF (diaPASEF).
- SWATH-MS was introduced by Gillet et al. (Aebersold lab, 2012) with SCIEX.

attrs.mnemonic: DIA = 'fragment everything, sort it out later' – like recording the whole concert instead of only the loudest solos.

items.gloss_md: Chemical tags of identical total mass attached to peptides from different samples, which are pooled and measured together; on fragmentation each tag releases a reporter ion of distinct mass that quantifies each sample.
items.body_md:
- Tags react with peptide N-termini and lysines (NHS esters); reporter ions appear in the low m/z range of MS2 (or MS3) spectra.
- Multiplexing: iTRAQ 4- and 8-plex; TMT 6/10/11-plex, TMTpro 16- and 18-plex (and higher-plex versions); samples are combined early, reducing missing values within a plex.
- Problem: ratio compression from co-isolated interfering peptides (true fold changes appear smaller) – mitigated by SPS-MS3, narrow isolation, real-time search; between-plex comparisons need a common reference channel.
- Widely used in deep tissue proteomics (e.g. CPTAC tumour cohorts including PDAC) and phosphoproteomics.

attrs.mnemonic: Isobaric = 'same weight in, different weight out': identical tags in MS1, distinct reporter ions in MS2.

items.gloss_md: Proteomics quantification without isotopic or chemical labels, comparing peptide signal intensities (or spectral counts) between separately measured samples.
items.body_md:
- Intensity-based: MS1 peak areas (DDA with match-between-runs) or fragment intensities (DIA); normalisation and protein roll-up e.g. MaxLFQ (Cox et al. 2014), directLFQ, iBAQ for within-sample abundance estimates.
- Spectral counting (number of MS2 spectra per protein) is a cruder older approach.
- Strengths: unlimited number of samples, simple sample preparation, any sample type; with DIA the method of choice for large clinical cohorts.
- Challenges: requires stable LC-MS performance over long series (QC samples, batch design), missing values (imputation choices), run-order effects.

items.label_md: SILAC (stable isotope labelling by amino acids in cell culture)
items.gloss_md: Metabolic labelling for quantitative proteomics in which cells are grown in media containing heavy-isotope arginine and lysine, so 'light' and 'heavy' proteomes can be mixed and compared within one MS run.
items.body_md:
- Heavy 13C/15N-Lys and -Arg ensure every tryptic peptide (ending in K or R) carries a label; mass shift pairs appear in MS1.
- Very accurate because samples are mixed at the earliest step; 2- or 3-plex (light/medium/heavy).
- Limited to cultured cells (or SILAC mice, at high cost); "super-SILAC" mixes of labelled cell lines serve as spike-in standards for tissue.
- Introduced by Ong et al. (Mann lab), 2002.

items.gloss_md: MS methods that measure a predefined set of peptides with high sensitivity and precision, typically with isotope-labelled peptide standards for absolute quantification.
items.body_md:
- SRM/MRM (selected/multiple reaction monitoring) on triple quadrupoles monitors specific precursor → fragment transitions; PRM (parallel reaction monitoring) records full fragment spectra on high-resolution instruments.
- Stable-isotope-labelled (heavy) peptides spiked in act as internal standards (AQUA); assays designed with Skyline.
- Uses: verification of biomarker candidates, clinical assays (e.g. thyroglobulin in the presence of autoantibodies), pathway quantification; also the basis of LC-MS/MS drug monitoring.
- Nature Methods Method of the Year 2012.

items.gloss_md: MS-based proteome-wide identification and quantification of protein phosphorylation sites after phosphopeptide enrichment, used to read out kinase signalling.
items.body_md:
- Enrichment with IMAC (Fe3+/Ti4+ metal ions) or TiO2, or antibody enrichment for phosphotyrosine; tens of thousands of sites per experiment.
- Site localisation scores (e.g. PTM localisation probability) decide which residue (Ser/Thr/Tyr) carries the phosphate.
- Kinase activity inference (e.g. KSEA, PTM-SEA) links sites to kinases such as MAPK/ERK downstream of KRAS, mTOR, or drug targets.
- Related PTM-omics: ubiquitinomics (di-Gly remnant enrichment), acetylomics, glycoproteomics.

items.gloss_md: Affinity proteomics in which each protein is recognised by a pair of antibodies carrying DNA oligos; only when both bind the same protein do the oligos hybridise and get extended into a DNA reporter that is quantified by qPCR or NGS.
items.body_md:
- Dual recognition gives high specificity; DNA readout allows high multiplexing from ~1–6 µL of plasma/serum.
- Panels: Target 96 and Flex (qPCR readout), Explore 3072 and Explore HT (~5,400 proteins, NGS readout); output NPX (Normalized Protein eXpression, relative log2 units – not absolute concentrations).
- Used in large cohorts (UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project ~3,000 proteins in >50,000 participants), biomarker discovery in inflammation, liver disease and oncology, protein QTL studies.
- Limitations: relative quantification, plate/batch effects (bridging samples needed), epitope effects (protein-altering variants can change binding).
- Olink (Uppsala, Sweden) was acquired by Thermo Fisher Scientific in 2024. PEA described by Lundberg et al. 2011.

attrs.mnemonic: PEA = two antibodies must 'shake hands' (their DNA tails meet) before there is any signal.

items.gloss_md: Affinity proteomics platform measuring ~7,000–11,000 proteins in small plasma volumes using SOMAmers – chemically modified DNA aptamers that bind specific proteins – read out on DNA microarrays.
items.body_md:
- SOMAmer = slow off-rate modified aptamer; modified nucleotides (hydrophobic side chains) increase affinity and specificity.
- Steps: binding in plasma → capture and wash steps → release of bound SOMAmers → hybridisation to arrays; output RFU (relative fluorescence units), normalised (ANML).
- Versions: v4.0 (~5,000), v4.1 (~7,000), 11K assay (~11,000 proteins).
- Uses: large epidemiological cohorts, pQTL studies, risk scores (e.g. for cardiovascular disease), MASLD/fibrosis biomarker discovery.
- Caveats: some reagents cross-react or bind protein complexes/isoforms differently; correlation with Olink varies widely between proteins; relative units.
- Developed by SomaLogic (Gold et al., PLoS One 2010); SomaLogic merged with Standard BioTools in 2024.

items.gloss_md: Plate-based immunoassay in which an antigen is captured and detected by antibodies coupled to an enzyme whose colour (or light) reaction is proportional to the amount of antigen.
items.body_md:
- Formats: sandwich (capture antibody on the plate + detection antibody; most common for proteins in serum), direct, indirect (detects antibodies, e.g. serology for hepatitis viruses), competitive (small molecules).
- Detection: HRP or alkaline phosphatase with colorimetric (TMB, read at 450 nm), fluorescent or chemiluminescent substrates; quantification against a standard curve, typically fitted with a 4- or 5-parameter logistic model.
- Sensitivity typically pg/mL–ng/mL; high-sensitivity successors: electrochemiluminescence (Meso Scale Discovery), Simoa digital ELISA (Quanterix, fg/mL), automated clinical chemiluminescence analysers (e.g. Roche Elecsys).
- Strengths: specific, quantitative, cheap, standardised; limitations: one analyte per well, depends on antibody pair quality, hook effect at very high concentrations, matrix interference (heterophile antibodies).

Invented in 1971 by Engvall and Perlmann (Stockholm) and independently by van Weemen and Schuurs (Netherlands).

attrs.mnemonic: Sandwich ELISA: bread (capture antibody) – filling (antigen) – bread (detection antibody) – and the enzyme is the ketchup that makes the colour.
attrs.anecdote: ELISA replaced radioimmunoassay (RIA), for which Rosalyn Yalow received the 1977 Nobel Prize; enzyme labels removed the need for radioactivity.

items.gloss_md: Protein detection method in which proteins are separated by size with SDS-PAGE, transferred to a membrane and detected with specific antibodies, confirming identity by molecular weight and giving semi-quantitative abundance.
items.body_md:
- Steps: lysis → SDS-PAGE (denatured, negatively charged proteins migrate by size) → electrotransfer to nitrocellulose or PVDF → blocking (milk/BSA) → primary antibody → HRP- or fluorophore-conjugated secondary → chemiluminescence (ECL) or fluorescence imaging.
- Molecular weight markers show size; isoforms, cleavage products (e.g. cleaved caspase-3, PARP), and post-translational modifications (phospho-specific antibodies, e.g. p-ERK vs total ERK) are distinguished.
- Normalisation: loading controls (β-actin, GAPDH, α-tubulin) or better total-protein staining; quantify only in the linear range.
- Limitations: low throughput, semi-quantitative, antibody specificity problems, image manipulation concerns (journals require raw blots). Automated capillary western: ProteinSimple Jess/Wes.

Described by Towbin et al. (1979); named "Western" by W. Neal Burnette (1981).

attrs.mnemonic: SNOW DROP: Southern – DNA, Northern – RNA, Western – Protein.
attrs.anecdote: According to W. Neal Burnette's own recollection, his 1981 paper naming the 'Western' blot was first rejected by another journal; he chose the name as a nod to Southern's DNA blot and the Northern RNA blot – and because his lab was in Seattle, on the West Coast.

items.gloss_md: Antibody-based proteomics in which many sample lysates are printed as tiny spots on a slide and each slide is probed with one validated antibody, measuring hundreds of proteins and phospho-proteins across hundreds of samples.
items.body_md:
- "Reverse" because the sample (not the antibody) is immobilised, opposite to forward-phase antibody arrays; dilution series of each lysate allow quantification in the linear range.
- Typical panels: ~200–500 well-validated antibodies, many against phosphorylated signalling proteins (AKT, mTOR, MAPK pathways).
- Requires little material; high throughput; limited by antibody availability and specificity.
- The MD Anderson RPPA core profiled TCGA tumours; data in The Cancer Proteome Atlas (TCPA).

items.gloss_md: Multiplex immunoassays in which colour-coded microbeads, each carrying a different capture antibody or antigen, are read in a flow-based or imaging analyser, measuring up to dozens of analytes in one small sample.
items.body_md:
- Each bead region has a unique internal dye ratio (up to 500 regions on FLEXMAP 3D); a reporter (phycoerythrin-labelled detection antibody) quantifies the analyte; magnetic beads simplify washing.
- Research use: cytokine/chemokine panels (e.g. IL-6, TNF, IL-10) from serum, plasma or supernatants.
- Transplantation: Luminex single antigen bead (SAB) assays with beads coated with individual HLA class I/II molecules detect and characterise anti-HLA antibodies and donor-specific antibodies (DSA) before and after transplantation; strength reported as mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) – central to virtual crossmatching and the diagnosis of antibody-mediated rejection.
- Limitations of SAB: semi-quantitative MFI, prozone effect (complement interference, fixed by EDTA/DTT treatment), denatured antigens.
- Luminex Corporation was acquired by DiaSorin in 2021.

attrs.mnemonic: Luminex = a box of coloured marbles: the marble's colour says what is measured, the PE glow says how much.

items.gloss_md: Pull-down of a specific protein from a lysate with an antibody bound to beads (protein A/G or magnetic), used to enrich the protein or, in co-immunoprecipitation, to find its binding partners.
items.body_md:
- Workflow: lyse under non-denaturing conditions → antibody + protein A/G beads → washes → elution → detection by Western blot or mass spectrometry (IP-MS / affinity purification–MS for interactomes).
- Co-IP shows physical association in cells but not necessarily direct binding; controls: IgG isotype IP, input, reciprocal IP.
- The same principle underlies ChIP (chromatin), RIP/CLIP (RNA–protein) and MeDIP (methylated DNA).

items.gloss_md: Genome-wide mapping of where a transcription factor or histone modification binds DNA: chromatin is crosslinked, fragmented, immunoprecipitated with a specific antibody, and the co-precipitated DNA is sequenced.
items.body_md:
- Steps: formaldehyde crosslinking → sonication or MNase fragmentation → IP with antibody → reverse crosslinks → library → sequencing; an input (non-IP) control is essential.
- Analysis: peak calling (MACS2/3 for sharp TF and narrow marks, broad-peak modes or SICER for broad marks), differential binding (DiffBind), motif analysis (HOMER, MEME).
- Common histone marks: H3K4me3 (active promoters), H3K27ac (active enhancers and promoters), H3K4me1 (enhancers), H3K36me3 (transcribed gene bodies), H3K27me3 (Polycomb repression), H3K9me3 (heterochromatin).
- Limitations: needs ~10^5–10^7 cells, antibody quality decides everything, high background; CUT&RUN/CUT&Tag are lower-input alternatives.
- Large reference data: ENCODE, Roadmap Epigenomics, Blueprint.

Introduced in 2007 (Johnson et al.; Barski et al.; Robertson et al.).

attrs.mnemonic: H3K4me3 = 'start here' (promoter), H3K27ac = 'active now' (enhancer), H3K27me3 = 'locked' (Polycomb): K4 for Kick-off, K27ac for Action, K27me3 for Mute.

items.gloss_md: Cleavage Under Targets and Release Using Nuclease: an antibody-tethered protein A/G–micrococcal nuclease cuts DNA around a chromatin protein's binding sites in intact permeabilised cells, releasing the fragments for sequencing.
items.body_md:
- No crosslinking or sonication; works with ~10^3–10^5 cells; very low background, so only ~3–8 million reads per sample are needed.
- Suited to transcription factors and histone marks; commercial kits (EpiCypher CUTANA, Cell Signaling).
- Developed by Skene and Henikoff (eLife 2017, Fred Hutch); CUT&Tag followed in 2019.
- Mechanism: permeabilised cells are bound to beads, incubated with the primary antibody, then pA/G-MNase; calcium activates the nuclease, and cleaved fragments diffuse out of the nuclei.
- Spike-in E. coli DNA or nucleosome standards support normalisation.

aliases: cleavage under targets and release using nuclease

items.gloss_md: Cleavage Under Targets and Tagmentation: an antibody-tethered protein A–Tn5 transposase inserts sequencing adapters directly at the binding sites of a histone mark or chromatin protein, producing ready-to-amplify libraries from very few cells.
items.body_md:
- One-tube workflow, works from ~hundreds to thousands of cells and at single-cell level (scCUT&Tag, combined with 10x or combinatorial indexing).
- Best for abundant histone marks (H3K27me3, H3K4me3, H3K27ac); weaker for transcription factors, and Tn5's preference for open chromatin can bias signals.
- Kaya-Okur et al., Nature Communications 2019 (Henikoff lab).
- Because adapters are inserted in situ, no separate library preparation is needed; reads per sample of a few million suffice.
- Peak calling with SEACR or MACS2.

items.gloss_md: Assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing: a hyperactive Tn5 transposase inserts sequencing adapters preferentially into open (nucleosome-free) chromatin, mapping accessible regulatory elements genome-wide.
items.body_md:
- Simple and fast: ~50,000 cells (or nuclei; Omni-ATAC improved signal and works on frozen tissue), tagmentation, PCR, sequencing.
- Output: peaks at promoters and enhancers; fragment-size distribution shows nucleosome-free (<100 bp) and mono-/di-nucleosome fragments; TF footprints and motif enrichment (chromVAR) infer which transcription factors are active.
- QC: TSS enrichment score, fraction of reads in peaks, mitochondrial read fraction (Tn5 loves mtDNA).
- Predecessors: DNase-seq, FAIRE-seq, MNase-seq; single-cell and Multiome versions exist.

Buenrostro et al., Nature Methods 2013 (Greenleaf and Chang labs, Stanford).

attrs.mnemonic: ATAC = Tn5 'attacks' only where the chromatin door is open.

items.gloss_md: DNA methylation profiling at single-base resolution: sodium bisulfite converts unmethylated cytosines to uracil (read as T), while methylated cytosines (5mC) remain C, so methylation is read from C/T differences after sequencing.
items.body_md:
- WGBS (whole-genome bisulfite sequencing): all ~28 million CpGs, needs ~30× coverage, gold standard.
- RRBS (reduced representation): MspI digestion (CCGG) enriches CpG islands and promoters, cheaper; targeted capture panels also exist.
- Bisulfite damages and fragments DNA; enzymatic methyl-seq (EM-seq: TET2 + APOBEC) is a gentler alternative; long-read platforms (ONT, PacBio) read 5mC natively.
- Bisulfite cannot distinguish 5mC from 5hmC (oxBS-seq or TAB-seq can).
- Analysis: Bismark/bwa-meth alignment, methylation β = methylated/(methylated + unmethylated) per CpG; DMR calling (DSS, methylKit).
- Clinical: cell-free DNA methylation for multi-cancer early detection and tissue-of-origin; methylation markers such as MGMT promoter (glioma).

attrs.mnemonic: Bisulfite turns the 'naked' (unmethylated) C into T; methylated C wears a hat (methyl group) and stays C.

items.gloss_md: Bead arrays that measure DNA methylation at hundreds of thousands of predefined CpG sites from bisulfite-converted DNA, the workhorse for epigenome-wide association studies and methylation-based tumour classification.
items.body_md:
- Versions: HumanMethylation27, 450K (~485,000 CpGs, 2011), MethylationEPIC v1 (~850,000, 2016), EPIC v2 (~935,000, 2022/2023); also smaller screening and mouse arrays.
- Two probe designs: Infinium I (two bead types per CpG) and Infinium II (one bead type, single-base extension); their different β distributions need normalisation (BMIQ, SWAN, Noob, functional normalisation).
- Output: β-values (0–1, ≈ fraction methylated) and M-values (log2 ratio, better for statistics). Analysis: minfi, SeSAMe, ChAMP.
- Applications: EWAS (e.g. MASLD, smoking), epigenetic clocks (Horvath 2013 pan-tissue clock; GrimAge), blood cell-type deconvolution (Houseman), copy-number from intensities, and diagnostic tumour classification – the DKFZ/Heidelberg brain tumour classifier (Capper et al., Nature 2018) and sarcoma classifier.
- Works with FFPE DNA (with restoration step) and low input.

attrs.anecdote: The Heidelberg methylation classifier for brain tumours (Capper et al. 2018) changed the diagnosis in about 12 % of cases compared with standard histopathology, and its web tool is now used worldwide.

items.gloss_md: Mapping of open chromatin by limited digestion of nuclei with DNase I, which cuts preferentially in nucleosome-free regulatory regions, followed by sequencing of the cut sites.
items.body_md:
- DNase I hypersensitive sites (DHSs) mark promoters, enhancers, insulators; high-depth DNase-seq reveals TF footprints.
- Workhorse of ENCODE and Roadmap Epigenomics (DHS maps across hundreds of cell types), now largely replaced by the simpler, lower-input ATAC-seq.
- Genome-wide method from 2006–2008 (Crawford et al.; Boyle et al.), based on hypersensitivity assays from the late 1970s.
- Requires many cells and careful titration of DNase I digestion, which explains why the simpler ATAC-seq replaced it in most labs.

items.gloss_md: Genome-wide method for the 3D organisation of chromatin: crosslinked DNA is digested, spatially close ends are ligated (proximity ligation), and ligation junctions are sequenced to give a contact map of all loci.
items.body_md:
- Reveals A/B compartments (active vs inactive chromatin), topologically associating domains (TADs) and CTCF/cohesin-anchored loops connecting enhancers and promoters.
- Family: 3C (one-to-one, Dekker 2002), 4C (one-to-all), 5C, Hi-C (all-to-all, Lieberman-Aiden et al., Science 2009), in situ Hi-C, Micro-C (MNase, nucleosome resolution), HiChIP/PLAC-seq (protein-centric), single-cell Hi-C.
- Uses: enhancer–gene assignment for GWAS variants, structural variant detection in cancer (translocations show as off-diagonal blocks), genome scaffolding for assemblies.
